contributions.text_english: Good afternoon and welcome to Wednesday's Plenary session. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy. Question 1, Vikki Howells.
contributions.text_original: Prynhawn da. Croeso i sesiwn ddydd Mercher. Cwestiynau i'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Fenter, Cysylltedd ac Ynni. Cwestiwn 1, Vikki Howells.

contributions.text_english: 1. What are the Welsh Government's priorities for improving access to public transport in Pontypridd Cynon Merthyr? OQ64484
contributions.text_original: 1. Beth yw blaenoriaethau Llywodraeth Cymru ar gyfer gwella mynediad at drafnidiaeth gyhoeddus ym Mhontypridd Cynon Merthyr? OQ64484

contributions.text_english: Thank you for the question, Vikki. We want to make it easier for more people to travel on buses and trains in Pontypridd Cynon Merthyr. That means better connections between bus and rail, keeping fares fair and providing reliable services. The south Wales metro is central to this work. We are also investing in improving local bus services and improving interchanges such as Merthyr.
contributions.text_original: Diolch am y cwestiwn, Vikki. Rydyn ni eisiau ei gwneud hi’n haws i fwy o bobl deithio ar fws ac ar drên ym Mhontypridd Cynon Merthyr. Mae hyn yn golygu bysiau a threnau sy’n gweithio’n well gyda’i gilydd, prisiau teg, a gwasanaethau sy’n dod ar amser. Mae metro de Cymru yn rhan bwysig o’r gwaith hwn. Rydyn ni hefyd yn rhoi arian i wella bysiau lleol a llefydd fel gorsaf Merthyr.

contributions.text_english: Thank you, Deputy Minister. Now, capping bus fares at £2 for adults was a key pledge in my party's manifesto from May, building on our work in Government, where we introduced £1 bus fares for young people and provided free bus travel for older people and people with disabilities. Now, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has announced that, from January 2027, single bus fares in England will be capped at £2 for adults. This will, of course, mean a Barnett consequential for the Welsh Government. So, will you use this to introduce a similar £2 cap for fares in Wales? And if not, will you explain why bus users in Wales should lose out?
contributions.text_original: Thank you, Deputy Minister. Now, capping bus fares at £2 for adults was a key pledge in my party's manifesto from May, building on our work in Government, where we introduced £1 bus fares for young people and provided free bus travel for older people and people with disabilities. Now, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has announced that, from January 2027, single bus fares in England will be capped at £2 for adults. This will, of course, mean a Barnett consequential for the Welsh Government. So, will you use this to introduce a similar £2 cap for fares in Wales? And if not, will you explain why bus users in Wales should lose out?

contributions.text_english: This Government is committed to buses being a key part of the transport infrastructure, especially for those people who maybe cannot afford and don't have access to a private car. We've made sure that the bus fare for young people is continued and that's a commitment throughout the term of this Government. It was in the programme for government that we talked about yesterday. We're looking forward to seeing the consequentials come in, but, as an ex-Minister, you know that the consequentials come into the Government, the Government then decides on the priorities it sets to that. You've seen the priorities in the programme for government yesterday. But if I can give you one reassurance, I think that bus services are one of the key things that this Government will be differentiating itself for over the next four years, because we recognise the importance of them to those people who are furthest away from their own transport solutions.

contributions.text_english: Minister, many people in Pontypridd Cynon Merthyr still struggle to access jobs, education and healthcare because of poor transport links. Given the significant amount of public money already spent on transport projects in Wales, can the Cabinet Secretary please explain why so many communities remain poorly served, and what steps will be taken to improve reliability and accessibility before asking taxpayers to fund further major schemes? Thank you.
contributions.text_original: Minister, many people in Pontypridd Cynon Merthyr still struggle to access jobs, education and healthcare because of poor transport links. Given the significant amount of public money already spent on transport projects in Wales, can the Cabinet Secretary please explain why so many communities remain poorly served, and what steps will be taken to improve reliability and accessibility before asking taxpayers to fund further major schemes? Thank you.

contributions.text_english: Thank you for the question, David. I think the key thing for this is actually starting to recognise the truth of the matter. We've got a Transport for Wales service that's hitting its time targets ahead of everyone else in the UK. The latest statistics show that Transport for Wales was hitting over 80 per cent within three minutes of its required time. So, it is providing the service it needs to provide. The second part of this is about making sure we have the funding to be able to invest in that infrastructure. If I remember, when we talked about rail devolution when I came to this Siambr relatively recently, the benches behind me were against us having extra rail devolution, which is for precisely the same reasons that you're asking the questions. We want to make sure that people can access jobs, healthcare and just make society work. I'm just going to reiterate a point I made to Vikki a few seconds ago. This is important for us in terms of not just rail transport, it's important to us from a bus perspective as well, and I think that's going to be key for these four years ahead.

contributions.text_english: Parents and children across Rhondda Cynon Taf are concerned about the impact of the council's decisions, which is a Labour-led council, to make school transport as complex as possible for children who just want to know whether they're going to get to school safely. The impact of this decision is significant. It affects local people who can't get on the bus because it is full of school pupils on their way to school and pupil attendance has been gravely affected. More concerning still, children can't go to the school they want to go to, including Welsh-medium schools, because there are fewer buses available or because of changes to the terms of the Learner Travel (Wales) Measure 2008. Deputy Minister, will you make a statement today supporting parents in RCT who want to make the Labour-led council prioritise the safety of children?
contributions.text_original: Mae rhieni a phlant ar draws Rhondda Cynon Taf yn pryderu am effeithiau penderfyniad y cyngor, sydd o dan arweiniad Llafur, i wneud cludiant ysgol mor gymhleth â phosib i blant sydd jest eisiau gofyn, 'A ydw i'n mynd i gyrraedd yr ysgol yn ddiogel?' Mae canlyniadau'r penderfyniad yma yn sylweddol. Mae'n effeithio ar bobl leol sydd ddim yn gallu mynd ar y bws oherwydd ei fod yn llawn disgyblion ar y ffordd i'r ysgol ac mae presenoldeb disgyblion yn yr ysgol wedi'i effeithio'n ddifrifol. Yn fwy pryderus byth, mae plant yn methu mynd i'r ysgol maen nhw eisiau, gan gynnwys ysgolion cyfrwng Cymraeg, oherwydd bod llai o fysiau ar gael neu oherwydd newidiadau i delerau'r Mesur Teithio gan Ddysgwyr (Cymru) 2008. Dirprwy Weinidog, a wnewch chi wneud datganiad heddiw yn cefnogi rhieni Rhondda Cynon Taf sydd am wneud i'r cyngor, sydd o dan arweiniad Llafur, flaenoriaethu diogelwch plant?

contributions.text_english: Thank you for the question, Lis.
contributions.text_original: Diolch am y cwestiwn, Lis.

contributions.text_english: I think there are a couple of things here. One, it's very complicated. I think one of the things that learner travel has shown me is that this is probably the biggest difficult problem I've got on my horizon, excepting that I've got the M4 and the Menai on that as well. So, it shows the complexity of it. And I think it's been shown by this Government that we've taken this on as a cross-portfolio opportunity, because, as you say, this affects—. We're talking about education and Welsh learner education, but also post-16 education. And one of the things that I found most disconcerting is that, ultimately, learner travel and learner transport should be an enabler of people's education; it should not be a disenabler. So, this Government is keen and it was in our 100-day commitment. We've started work on it, particularly in relation to the Welsh language first, but then we're going to be focusing on post-16 education and, following that, it'll be additional learning needs learner transport as well.

contributions.text_english: 2. How will the Welsh Government's energy policy support its efforts to achieve its net-zero targets? OQ64525
contributions.text_original: 2. Sut y bydd polisi ynni Llywodraeth Cymru yn cefnogi ei hymdrechion i gyflawni ei thargedau sero net? OQ64525

contributions.text_english: The Welsh Government’s national energy strategy will take a whole-systems approach, replacing the previous renewable electricity generation target with an emissions-based energy target. This will help identify where action delivers the greatest contribution to our ambition of achieving net zero by 2040.
contributions.text_original: The Welsh Government’s national energy strategy will take a whole-systems approach, replacing the previous renewable electricity generation target with an emissions-based energy target. This will help identify where action delivers the greatest contribution to our ambition of achieving net zero by 2040.

contributions.text_english: Thank you, Minister. Minister, releasing carbon dioxide into the atmosphere causes temperatures on earth to rise, and that isn't good for any of us. And we need to achieve whatever reduction in emissions is necessary to secure the long-term future of mankind. That's why, in its current formulation, net zero is so frustrating. Deindustrialisation and a reliance on China and India are not long-term solutions. Renewables, again, are not a long-term solution, neither is burying our heads in the sand about the economic and geopolitical problems created by net zero. The only long-term solution to the challenges that we face, both as a nation and as a species, is nuclear power. So, I'm excited about the development of small modular reactors at Wylfa. After that, Minister, what's next for nuclear power in Wales?
contributions.text_original: Thank you, Minister. Minister, releasing carbon dioxide into the atmosphere causes temperatures on earth to rise, and that isn't good for any of us. Deindustrialisation and a reliance on China and India are not long-term solutions. Renewables, again, are not a long-term solution, neither is burying our heads in the sand about the economic and geopolitical problems created by net zero. The only long-term solution to the challenges that we face, both as a nation and as a species, is nuclear power. So, I'm excited about the development of small modular reactors at Wylfa. After that, Minister, what's next for nuclear power in Wales?

contributions.text_english:
I just would point out to the Member that I think the context is key here, isn't it?  So, the situation in Wales where we have unique assets—latent potential in many cases in terms of green energy—is that, actually, green energy is the means for our reindustrialisation, not our deindustrialisation. I'm specifically referring to, for example, our globally significant potential in terms of floating offshore wind, and the well-known, unique natural advantages we have in terms of tidal technologies, for example. We could, therefore, not just generate the electricity through those technologies, but also capture the supply chain and build up a manufacturing base on that level.

In relation to his point about nuclear, I would just point out that, actually, the move towards an emissions-based target includes not just renewable sectors, but also other low-carbon technologies that include nuclear, alongside carbon capture and storage.

contributions.text_english: I'm pleased to hear the Minister's reference to reindustrialisation. I welcome that. I would also agree on the importance of the nuclear industry in achieving that. Last week, I visited Hinkley Point, which is a nuclear power station that is being built with a great deal of Welsh steel, and there's an opportunity to go further, beyond the new project in Wylfa, in expanding nuclear in Wales.
contributions.text_original: Dwi'n falch o glywed cyfeiriad y Gweinidog at ailddiwydiannu. Dwi'n croesawu hynny. Byddwn hefyd yn eilio pwysigrwydd y diwydiant niwclear i gwblhau hynny. Yr wythnos diwethaf, bues i lawr yn Hinkley Point, pwerdy niwclear sydd wedi ei adeiladu gyda pheth helaeth o ddur Cymreig, ac mae yna gyfle i fynd ymhellach, y tu hwnt i'r prosiect newydd yn Wylfa, o ran ehangu'r diwydiant niwclear yng Nghymru.

contributions.text_english: But on the net-zero target set by Welsh Government for 2040, we welcome that target. We will push you on it. But that target is meaningless unless the Minister is prepared to deliver the renewable energy infrastructure needed to achieve it, and you referenced renewables in your earlier answer. Do you accept that Wales cannot reach net zero in that time frame without a major expansion of onshore wind as well as offshore wind, and that that in itself cannot be delivered without grid infrastructure and pylons to connect it? And if you do accept that premise, will you commit to supporting that infrastructure and those projects, even where those decisions prove difficult and locally unpopular?

contributions.text_english:
I'm grateful to the Member for his question. There are a number of elements to that question, but, of course, everything is connected at the end of the day, isn't it?

With the national energy strategy, one of the major elements will be setting out the different contributions that will be made by each form of technology, and then, of course, at a spatial level—so, that's one aspect—and setting out what the different elements will contribute. The decision with regard to Gwyndod, to all intents and purposes, has already been made, and that's the basis on which all of the energy stakeholders across Britain are planning.

That element has to be a part of the mix, but, certainly, we do accept that there is a contribution to be made by onshore green energy, and there are implications in terms of ensuring that the infrastructure with regard to grid connection is there to facilitate that to happen in the most efficient way with regard to our systems and our economy, recognising, of course, that there is a need in any planning framework to strike the right balance in terms of the interests and voice of the community.
contributions.text_original:
Rwy'n ddiolchgar i'r Aelod am ei gwestiwn. Mae yna nifer o elfennau yn fanna, ond, wrth gwrs, mae popeth yn gysylltiedig ar ddiwedd y dydd, onid ydy? 

Gyda'r strategaeth ynni genedlaethol, wrth gwrs, un o'r elfennau mawr fydd gosod mas y gwahanol gyfraniadau fydd yn cael eu gwneud fesul technoleg, a wedyn, wrth gwrs, ar lefel gofodol—so, bydd hwnna’n elfen—a gosod mas beth mae’r gwahanol elfennau yn cyfrannu. Mae’r penderfyniad gyda Gwyndod, i bob pwrpas, wedi’i wneud, a dyna’r sail y mae’r holl randdeiliaid ynni ar draws Prydain nawr yn cynllunio arni.

Felly, mae’r elfen yna, wrth gwrs, yn gorfod bod yn rhan ohono fe, ond, yn sicr, rŷn ni’n derbyn bod cyfraniad gydag ynni gwyrdd ar y tir, ac mae yna oblygiadau wedyn o ran sicrhau bod y seilwaith o ran cysylltiadau grid yno i helpu hynny i ddigwydd yn y ffordd fwyaf effeithlon o ran ein systemau ni, a hefyd o ran ein economi, gan, wrth gwrs, gydnabod bod yna angen gydag unrhyw fframwaith cynllunio i gael y balans yn iawn o ran y llais a'r buddiannau cymunedol hefyd.

contributions.text_english: Good afternoon, Minister.
contributions.text_original: Prynhawn da, Weinidog.

contributions.text_english:
I'm really pleased to hear from Reform UK that there's not a rejection of the net-zero targets, which we have previously heard. So, I'm hoping that there's been a bit of a change on those benches over there. But I would like just to come back on the point that was made by Joe Martin in relation to selective forms of energy, because what we should be doing is everything. The world is on fire. We've seen the wildfires across Wales this summer, and, actually, we have at our fingertips the opportunity to deliver a whole raft of renewable energy, and here in Wales, as you've said, we've got a real opportunity.

Very different to my friend on my right—you're not on the right, I know—. We've talked about this before, but I would like to give you another opportunity, just to be clear on this, that, in developing onshore wind, your commitment still is to undergrounding those transmission cables, because that's what our communities want. I'm hoping you'll confirm that, and also that we're looking at how communities can own that onshore wind as well. Diolch yn fawr iawn.

I'm grateful to the Member for her question, and she is absolutely right, of course, that our national energy strategy will be looking particularly at those technologies where Wales is well placed, in terms of its natural assets, in the way that I described, to develop. But we need to be mindful, of course, of nascent technologies, which are at different stages of maturity at any point. So, this area never stands still, and we need to be building the capacity for Wales to be a test bed for some of those technologies that are on the horizon as well. 

In relation to grid infrastructure, can I take the opportunity as well to say—I should be able to recite this without looking at my notes—that we are clearly committed to delivering our manifesto commitment in relation to the distribution network of 132 kV and below, which is in favour of undergrounding, with only exceptions in terms of overhead, through low wooden poles, or other similar, equally unintrusive infrastructure?

contributions.text_english: Thank you. I now call the party spokespeople to question the Cabinet Minister. The Reform UK spokesperson, Jason O'Connell.
contributions.text_original: Diolch. Galwaf yn awr ar lefarwyr y pleidiau i holi. Llefarydd Reform UK, Jason O'Connell.

contributions.text_english: Diolch, Ddirprwy Lywydd. Minister, this week marks three years since the introduction of the default 20 mph limit across Wales. That's three years that motorists have been treated as a problem, and three years since this institution has ignored all the calls to overturn this disastrous policy. The cost is 1 billion extra minutes to car journey times across Wales each year. That's 1 billion minutes, and a policy estimated to cost up to £9 billion to the Welsh economy. And, after all of that, Welsh road deaths are still rising throughout the varying speed zones. Now, Minister, every one of those deaths is a tragedy. Road safety deserves a strategy that's more than just changing road signs. For years, when Labour was in Government, your party backed this single-minded approach. You defended it, you backed it, and now the data tells us it's clearly not working. So, Cabinet Minister, will you finally listen to the data and the hundreds of thousands of people who continue to speak out against this policy and end this experiment?

contributions.text_english: I hesitate to thank you for the question, Jason, but I will do out of courtesy. At the business statement last week, you were reminded to use data carefully, and you used the same data now as you used then. This data doesn't relate to 20 mph. Let's give you the actual data: in 2025, there were 1,469 collisions on roads with 20 mph and 30 mph speed limits combined, which is 2 per cent higher than in 2024, when there were 1,445. But it is the second lowest annual number ever recorded in Wales. So, this proves that, when we've reduced speed limits, it's actually reduced collisions. And I've heard it from people over the other side of the Siambr, and I appreciate it. This saves children's lives. This is a policy that this Government supports. We recognise there were ways we could have done it better; we talked about that throughout the last term, and I think we'd say the same thing again. However, we've got to make sure we follow the evidence, and when the evidence gets polluted by words that aren't actually true, it distorts things. The one thing that I'm sure that I'm going to make sure I do is that I am evidence led; I'm not going to be just led by rhetoric that is from the benches behind.

contributions.text_english:
I'm pretty sure I heard the data tell me there that accidents were going up, but that's the data for you.

Cabinet Minister, you can dispute all the figures you like, but you can't dispute your party's own record. This goes far beyond the 20 mph default limit. For years, major road projects have been frozen, cancelled or ruled out while congestion's got worse and motorists have been left in traffic up and down Wales. Your own leader made his priorities perfectly clear during the election campaign. He said that Plaid would keep the default limit and that it would not be reviewed. So, let us be clear: while we accept that this is a policy that you inherited from the previous Government, it's an approach you actively supported. You spent years telling the people of Wales that this was all about safety, when in fact, as most people know, up and down the country, it was all about the pursuit of damaging net-zero dogma. Absolutely. Without the proper infrastructure investment, frustrated Welsh motorists would have no choice but to use public transport—isn't that right, Minister? So, rather than punishing motorists as a transport strategy, will you actually invest in the proper road infrastructure that Wales actually needs?

contributions.text_english: Minister, data centres, I've written to you about them many a time, and, obviously, they're not new, but their use—principally because of AI and its expansion—is going to be important. There are critical challenges around that, potentially opportunities as well, in terms of jobs and growth and all the rest of it. To that end, it was really good to have a response from you. When I wrote to you, you responded about a new strategic policy framework for data centres in Wales. I think that's really critical, and of course it would be great to now, I guess, understand from you what the Government's intentions are on the basis of that framework. I'm sure that you would, hopefully, agree with me that we need to ensure that communities that have that infrastructure do then actually receive tangible local benefits through good jobs, good apprenticeships and genuine community wealth building.

contributions.text_english: I'm really grateful to the Member, not just for writing to me, as she's described, but also for raising this subject here in the Siambr, which gives me an opportunity to address some of the issues that are relevant to this area. It's important to acknowledge that with the huge growth of data centres, related digital infrastructure and the wider context, of course, of AI, edge computing and related technologies, we do need to have a robust policy framework that is futureproofed and that also recognises the need to enable us to have the advantages that can flow from the investments that are happening in digital infrastructure across the world but to do so in a way that balances those with the legitimate concerns that people have at a community level and more broadly in terms of energy use, in terms of water, in terms of land use et cetera. So, we will be setting this out as soon as we can so that we can have that discussion across the Siambr and more widely across civil society in Wales.

Diolch. I hope you can answer this one. Minister, the original plan was that £70 million of public money would help unlock around £330 million of private investment. For years, we were told there was serious private sector interest. GCRE talked about credible bidders and international interest, even from the middle east and America. And as recently as March last year, the First Minister at the time told this Senedd that GCRE was in detailed discussions with a potential funder, yet the private investment still hasn't materialised and the rail testing centre still hasn't been built.

So, what exactly went wrong? Was there ever an investor genuinely prepared to put up the money needed to build the project, and, if so, why did they walk away? Because, at this moment in time, it does look as though your Government has inherited a large hole in the ground, a project nobody is prepared to invest in, and, potentially, a very large bill for putting the site back as it was. How much more taxpayers' money are you prepared to put into this scheme? Diolch yn fawr.

contributions.text_english: 3. What role will community energy projects play in Wales's transition to net zero? OQ64557
contributions.text_original: 3. Pa rôl fydd prosiectau ynni cymunedol yn ei chwarae yn nhrawsnewidiad Cymru i sero net? OQ64557

contributions.text_english: Our national energy strategy will recognise the vital role of community energy in achieving net zero. The Welsh public energy company will help unlock that ambition, scaling up the number of community energy projects, installing renewables and storage and using them to provide lower cost power and heat to people.
contributions.text_original: Bydd ein strategaeth ynni genedlaethol yn cydnabod rôl hanfodol ynni cymunedol wrth gyflawni sero net. contributions.text_english: Thank you very much. It's excellent to hear that you share my view that community energy has a crucial role to play as we move towards our ambition of a net-zero Wales. Of course, at the heart of our principles as we develop community energy projects is that they align with local need, and it's important to ensure that the planning process reflects that. A perfect example of an industrial development that is contrary to our principles in my constituency is the Menai data centre scheme on the former Ferodo site near Caernarfon. It's a project that will swallow great amounts of energy and water, will have a damaging impact on wildlife and will cause sound and light pollution locally. But, more than anything, the huge scale of the project means that it will be sure to destroy our local landscapes and views, while offering very few local benefits. So, how can you ensure that the energy supply for data centres doesn't have a negative impact on the local area?
contributions.text_original: Diolch yn fawr iawn. Mae'n wych clywed eich bod chi o'r un farn â fi fod gan ynni cymunedol ran hollbwysig i'w chwarae wrth inni symud tuag at ein huchelgais o Gymru sero net. Wrth gwrs, wrth galon ein hegwyddorion wrth inni fynd ati i ddatblygu prosiectau ynni cymunedol yw eu bod nhw'n cyd-fynd â'r anghenion yn lleol, ac mae'n bwysig sicrhau bod y broses cynllunio yn adlewyrchu hynny. Enghraifft berffaith o ddatblygiad diwydiannol sydd yn mynd yn gwbl groes i'n hegwyddorion ni yn fy etholaeth i yw'r cynllun canolfan ddata Menai ar hen safle Ferodo yn ardal Caernarfon. Mae'n brosiect fydd yn llyncu llwythi o ynni a dŵr, yn cael effaith ddinistriol ar fywyd natur ac yn achosi llygredd sŵn a golau yn lleol. Ond, yn fwy na dim, mae graddfa anferthol y prosiect yn golygu y bydd yn siŵr o ddifetha ein tirwedd a'n golygfeydd yn lleol, gan gynnig ychydig iawn o fanteision yn lleol. Felly, sut y gallwch sicrhau nad yw cyflenwad ynni canolfannau data yn cael effaith negyddol ar yr ardal leol?

contributions.text_english: I'm grateful to the Member for that supplementary question. I think that you get to the core of the principles of our economic policy, namely that developments in terms of our economy or our energy system have to be planned for the benefit of the people of Wales. We have seen in our past as a nation, of course, the opposite of that happening, and developments taking place at the expense of local interests. We're not willing to see the same mistakes being made again. So, that's why we put an emphasis on community energy. We have made a commitment in terms of ensuring a minimum, at least, in terms of the local ownership of major projects, and in the particular context you referred to in terms of data centres, if I could echo what I said earlier, we as a Government will be bringing a policy framework forward that will address the quite understandable fears that exist across Wales where there are recommendations made in terms of data centres that don't give due consideration to the interests of local people or the local environment.
contributions.text_original: Dwi'n ddiolchgar i'r Aelod am y cwestiwn atodol. Rydyn ni wedi gweld yn ein gorffennol fel cenedl, wrth gwrs, y gwrthwyneb yn digwydd, a datblygiadau'n digwydd ar draul buddiannau pobl leol. Dydyn ni ddim yn barod i weld yr un camgymeriad yn digwydd eto. Felly, dyna pam rydyn ni'n rhoi pwyslais ar ynni cymunedol. Rydyn ni'n rhoi ymrwymiad o ran sicrhau isafswm, o leiaf, mewn prosiectau mawr o ran perchnogaeth leol, ac yn y cyd-destun penodol y gwnaethoch chi gyfeirio ato fe o ran canolfannau data, os caf i ategu'r hyn a ddywedais i'n gynharach, mi fyddwn ni fel Llywodraeth yn dod â fframwaith polisi gerbron sy'n mynd i'r afael â'r ofnau digon dealladwy ar draws Cymru lle mae yna argymhellion o ran canolfannau data sydd ddim yn rhoi'r priod ystyriaeth i fuddiannau pobl leol na'r amgylchedd lleol.

contributions.text_english: Cabinet Minister, there's a world of difference between genuine community energy and simply expecting rural communities to host enormous commercial energy developments. Across Wales, communities are being asked to accept industrial-scale windfarms, pylons and other infrastructure, while too often the electricity profits and the economic benefits flow elsewhere. So, if your Government wants at least 1.5 GW of renewable energy capacity to be locally owned by 2035, will you guarantee that community energy really means community ownership, community consent and tangible benefits for the people who live there, including lower energy costs, rather than simply imposing ever more large-scale development on rural Wales and calling a community benefit fund compensation? Diolch.

contributions.text_english: I'm grateful to the Member for his question. As I said a moment ago, I think that building, financing and facilitating community energy that is 100 per cent community owned is an important element of our policy. For larger schemes, we have said that we are committed to mandating a minimum level of community ownership of those schemes. I would say, more broadly, as well, a key principle of our national energy strategy will be taking an approach that I would characterise as more planned in relation to the spatial development of energy, rather than what we've had previously, which is, essentially, a market-led approach, which has led to concerns in communities, legitimate questions, like whether cumulative impact is properly being addressed. So, I think, by taking a planned approach, and getting the balance right between the necessity for decarbonising our energy system, recognising the range of technologies, including onshore renewables and their role in that, but giving confidence to communities as well that this is being done in a planned way, with them, and is not being imposed upon them with little benefit accruing to communities and to the people of Wales.

contributions.text_english: Improving economic outcomes in Ceredigion Penfro means backing local businesses, strengthening rural economies, and creating better paid jobs. contributions.text_english: Minister, thank you for your response. So, a simple question, Minister: are the defence growth deal and Aberporth both exempt from that pause? And if not, can you guarantee that not one job or contract, and not one pound of investment in Ceredigion Penfro will be lost or delayed as a result? West Wales needs certainty and investment now, not another framework standing in the way. Diolch.

Where there are decisions that—. We are trying—. Obviously, where it's possible to defer, partly out of respect for this Senedd, really—. So, we have that flexibility, and I can assure him, as the economy Minister, I will be mindful of the need to use that flexibility where necessary.

contributions.text_english: 6. How will the Cabinet Minister ensure that the benefits of the Welsh Government's new national energy strategy are retained within local communities? OQ64542
contributions.text_original: 6. Sut y bydd y Gweinidog Cabinet yn sicrhau bod manteision strategaeth ynni genedlaethol newydd Llywodraeth Cymru yn cael eu cadw o fewn cymunedau lleol? OQ64542

contributions.text_english: We are determined that the communities hosting energy developments are genuine beneficiaries. The national energy strategy will identify the clean energy that Wales needs and how more of this can be owned through minimum community ownership requirements and investment from the new Welsh public energy company.
contributions.text_original: We are determined that the communities hosting energy developments are genuine beneficiaries. The national energy strategy will identify the clean energy that Wales needs and how more of this can be owned through minimum community ownership requirements and investment from the new Welsh public energy company.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch. I welcome this Government's commitment to a renewable energy strategy that retains value in Welsh communities. The net-zero economy is already a significant and high-value component of the Welsh economy. There are particular opportunities in Ceredigion Penfro, with 1,600 jobs in the sector in Pembrokeshire alone already, and billions set to be invested in upcoming projects. This ranges from successful community-owned projects, such as Cwm Arian, to large-scale initiatives, like the Celtic Freeport.

Net zero is now an integral part of Welsh industry, and we've got huge potential to develop this further. The transition to net zero is a major economic opportunity, but I also welcome what the Minister has said here, that there needs to be a proper, planned strategy as to how we do this, both spatially and to balance the benefits for our economy, our communities and the environment. So, could the Cabinet Minister describe, as more energy infrastructure is developed in our rural communities, how Government will now ensure genuine benefit through local ownership jobs and skills and lower energy bills?

contributions.text_english: I'm really grateful for the question—part of an emerging theme this afternoon. It's such an important opportunity for us nationally and locally to make sure that we create an energy system where we benefit from the energy resources that we have. We can do that at different scales; we can do it through the Welsh public energy company at a larger scale, publicly owned, delivering benefit across the whole of Wales, for the people of Wales; we can do it through supporting community ownership, of which there are some good examples in the Member's constituency already. One of the reasons for doing that is precisely to get to grips with the energy costs problem that we face. Wales has some of the highest energy costs relatively compared to other parts of the UK. The UK has some of the highest energy costs in Europe. There's good evidence that community ownership actually is a means by which you can begin to deliver lower costs to households. And similarly, a publicly owned energy company, which is free not to follow the market price in energy, but to say, 'Let's actually engage in contracts with large-scale industrial users in Wales to create a Welsh energy advantage using our renewable energy resources, but for the benefit of our economy', that's precisely why we're creating a Welsh public energy company, and we're supporting public ownership and local ownership in a variety of ways at different scales.

contributions.text_english:
I welcome the Welsh Government's guidance published in June on behind-the-meter energy systems, and I was pleased to see the Government recognising the potential for businesses to generate, use and sell locally produced energy. These are exactly the sorts of arrangements that can deliver real economic benefit to Welsh communities and ensure that solar panels are installed on industrial units rather than prime agricultural land.

I have heard from business owners who tell me that the financial return from exporting surplus electricity to the grid can be low, that it's so low that it simply does not provide enough incentive to install solar panels on large commercial or industrial buildings. Suppliers setting their own export tariffs turns this on its head. So, can the Minister outline what they are doing to actively promote private-wire and licence-exempt arrangements, allowing businesses to sell surplus power directly to neighbouring businesses at an agreed price?

contributions.text_english: I'm really grateful to the Member for his question. He's absolutely right: I think that private-wire, behind-the-meter opportunities are actually one of the ways in which we can do what I just described, really, which is to create that energy advantage, particularly in the context of businesses. Because it can be done, there is a means to do it, but we've got to get organised to see where we can build that out at scale to facilitate businesses, because if they can avoid the network costs—. Although there's been some movement from the UK Government on network costs to large industrial users, by and large, there's still a huge network cost element. If we can devise different ways, it could be on-site microgeneration in some circumstances; in larger scales, there could be local energy systems, which are behind the wire, which could actually provide low-cost energy for a wide range of businesses. There's some work we've got to do with some of the stakeholders in order to ensure that the arrangement that you just described in terms of connection, maybe with the grid, can be part of it. So, we're working on it. It's absolutely one of the areas where, if we work smart, we could build that Welsh energy advantage, which will be such a critical determinant of our economic success.

contributions.text_english: 7. Will the Cabinet Minister provide an update on the performance of the Development Bank of Wales? OQ64545
contributions.text_original: 7. A wnaiff y Gweinidog Cabinet roi diweddariad am berfformiad Banc Datblygu Cymru? OQ64545

contributions.text_english: The Development Bank of Wales continues to deliver finance and investment support to businesses across Wales. The bank has reported strong performance during the year and remains a key economic development partner. Its 2025-26 annual report will be published later this month, setting out its full performance and economic impact.
contributions.text_original: The Development Bank of Wales continues to deliver finance and investment support to businesses across Wales. The bank has reported strong performance during the year and remains a key economic development partner. Its 2025-26 annual report will be published later this month, setting out its full performance and economic impact.

contributions.text_english: While of course I support ethical guidelines of conduct for the Development Bank of Wales, I worry about the politicisation of the bank and that investment decisions are based more off the whims of the Welsh Government rather than sensible financial criteria. For example, climate change is now a political priority that's been forced on the bank by the Government to meet mad net-zero targets. In the programme for government announced yesterday, we heard new economic criteria and possibly restrictions on defence investments for the bank. We have already had plenty of controversy with the bank in recent years, with concerns over political donations and alleged blacklisting of certain businesses. Can the Minister confirm whether the new defence ethical framework announced yesterday will apply to the Development Bank of Wales, and, if so, when? And will the Government publish a consolidated ethical and policy criteria that the development bank is expected to follow so that businesses and the Senedd can now understand how investment decisions are being made and scrutinise any further changes? Diolch.

And will the Government publish a consolidated ethical and policy criteria that the development bank is expected to follow so that businesses and the Senedd can now understand how investment decisions are being made and scrutinise any further changes? Diolch.

contributions.text_english:
I intend to issue the bank's remit letter in the coming weeks, which will set out clear priorities for the bank, supporting this Government's ambitions for investment, productivity and growth. That's a standard approach that every Government uses. There's nothing to see there. It's how every Government relates to arm's-length bodies, setting out the way in which the arm's-length body can deliver to the wider ambitions of the Government, particularly in the economic sphere.

Of course, we would expect the ethical framework that we are setting out in the defence sector to be cross-Government. It's there to govern the use of public money, including by the development bank, and it will also govern the development agency. Again, it's fairly normal. There are policies around fair work, for example. You would expect these to be reflected across the whole range of agencies.

I was at the launch of the development bank's Economic Intelligence Wales 'Productivity Heroes' report, and there's fantastic news here; let's remind ourselves of that. Over 1,700 high-growth firms are delivering higher productivity, higher employment and higher profits for those businesses so that they can continue to reinvest in their future trajectory of growth. I recognise scrutiny is an important part of our work here, but also let's not lose the opportunity to celebrate Welsh economic success. Because there are great things happening in Wales, and some of it is down to the work of the development bank.

contributions.text_english: Thank you. The final question to you, Minister. Question 8, Elfed Williams.
contributions.text_original: Y cwestiwn olaf i chi, Weinidog. Cwestiwn 8, Elfed Williams.

contributions.text_english: 8. What action is the Welsh Government taking to maximise the local economic opportunities arising from the Gwyndod project in Bangor Conwy Môn? OQ64550
contributions.text_original: 8. Pa gamau y mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn eu cymryd i wneud y mwyaf o’r cyfleoedd economaidd lleol sy’n deillio o brosiect Gwyndod ym Mangor Conwy Môn? OQ64550

contributions.text_english: The Welsh Government is working closely with Great British Energy—Nuclear and Rolls-Royce SMR to maximise local benefits from Gwyndod. We are helping Welsh businesses to access supply chain opportunities and working with education partners to enable local people to develop the required skills that will be required for the project.
contributions.text_original: Mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn cydweithio'n agos gyda Great British Energy—Nuclear a Rolls-Royce SMR i sicrhau'r manteision mwyaf posibl i'r gymuned leol o Gwyndod. Rydym yn cefnogi busnesau Cymru i ddefnyddio cyfleoedd y gadwyn gyflenwi ac yn gweithio gyda phartneriaid addysg i alluogi pobl leol i ddatblygu'r sgiliau sydd eu hangen ar gyfer y prosiect.

contributions.text_english: I thank the Cabinet Minister for that response. On my visit to the Gwyndod site last week, it was clear that this is not only an opportunity to secure energy for decades, but also a once-in-a-generation opportunity for the economy of Ynys Môn and north-west Wales. If we want local people to truly benefit, we need to start to prepare now. That means working with local colleges to ensure that apprenticeships and the required skills are in place, and, importantly, that they have the funding to deliver those. It also means giving fair opportunities to local businesses to get work through the supply chain. Will the Minister therefore commit to ensuring that jobs, skills and local businesses will be at the heart of the Welsh Government's strategy for Gwyndod? Thank you.
contributions.text_original: Diolch i'r Gweinidog Cabinet am yr ymateb. Ar fy ymweliad â safle Gwyndod yr wythnos diwethaf, roedd hi'n amlwg fod hwn nid yn unig yn gyfle i sicrhau ynni dibynadwy am ddegawdau, ond yn gyfle unwaith mewn cenedlaeth i economi Ynys Môn a'r gogledd-orllewin. Os ydym am i bobl leol elwa go iawn, mae angen dechrau paratoi nawr. Mae hynny'n golygu gweithio gyda'r colegau lleol i sicrhau prentisiaethau a'r sgiliau fydd eu hangen, ac, yn bwysig, sicrhau bod ganddynt y cyllid i wneud hynny. Mae hefyd yn golygu rhoi cyfle teg i fusnesau lleol ennill gwaith drwy'r gadwyn gyflenwi. A wnaiff y Gweinidog felly ymrwymo i sicrhau mai swyddi, sgiliau a busnesau lleol fydd wrth galon strategaeth Llywodraeth Cymru ar gyfer Gwyndod? Diolch.

contributions.text_english:
Certainly, this is a golden opportunity in terms of the economy of the whole of Wales, and also regionally and locally. We want to maximise the benefits of that opportunity across the range of dimensions in terms of skills. The Learning and Work Institute has been commissioned to carry out a skills review for Wales. In this context, Great British Energy—Nuclear has been invited to contribute to the call for evidence, so that the needs of the specific workforce for Gwyndod can be at the heart of the strategy that will emerge. The nuclear skills centre and a working group has been drawn together to bring together industry, the Welsh Government, local government and community representatives around a co-ordinated approach, to ensure that we have the system that we need in place to ensure that local people can derive the maximum benefit from the opportunities available.

In terms of the supply chain for local businesses, Welsh Government officials will be playing a central role in the Gwyndod suppliers event—and I'm pleased to publicise this more widely—that will be held over two days in Coleg Menai in Llangefni, on 22 and 23 October, alongside GBE-N and Rolls-Royce SMR. So, there is a great deal of work being done, but that's an overview of what's possible. It's another example, because the decision has already been made, of Wales's importance not just in terms of renewable energy—there are many opportunities in that regard in north Wales—but that we are also there at the beginning of this new technology of SMRs in the United Kingdom, and Wales is in a very good position to benefit economically from these for generations to come.
contributions.text_original:
Yn sicr, mae hwn yn gyfle euraid o ran economi Cymru gyfan, a hefyd yn rhanbarthol ac yn lleol. Rydym ni eisiau gwneud y mwyaf o'r cyfle hwnnw ar draws yr amrediad o ddimensiynau o ran sgiliau. Mae'r Sefydliad Dysgu a Gwaith wedi cael ei gomisiynu i wneud archwiliad sgiliau cenedlaethol ar gyfer Cymru. Yn y cyd-destun yma, mae GBE-N wedi cael ei wahodd i gyfrannu at y galw am dystiolaeth, fel y gall gyfynion y gweithlu penodol ar gyfer Gwyndod fod yn ganolog i'r strategaeth a ddaw yn ei sgil. Mae canolfan sgiliau niwclear Cymru a grŵp llywio wedi'u sefydlu i ddod â diwydiant, Llywodraeth Cymru, llywodraeth leol, darparwyr a chymunedau ynghyd o amgylch dull cydlynol, i sicrhau bod gyda ni y system sydd ei hangen er mwyn sicrhau bod pobl leol yn cael y mwyaf o'r cyfle sydd yno.

O ran y gadwyn gyflenwi ar gyfer busnesau lleol, bydd swyddogion Llywodraeth Cymru yn chwarae rôl ganolog mewn digwyddiad cyflenwyr Gwyndod—mae'n falch gen i geisio hysbysu hynny yn fwy eang—a fydd yn digwydd dros ddau ddiwrnod yng Ngholeg Menai yn Llangefni ar 22 a 23 Hydref, ochr yn ochr â GBE-N a Rolls-Royce SMR. Felly, mae yna lot mwy yn digwydd, ond dyma ryw fraslun o'r hyn sy'n bosib. Mae'n enghraifft arall, gan fod y penderfyniad wedi cael ei wneud, o sut mae Cymru yn bwysig nid yn unig o ran ynni adnewyddol—ac mae yna lot o gyfleoedd fanna yng ngogledd Cymru—ond ein bod ni hefyd yno ar ddechrau technoleg newydd o ran SMR ym Mhrydain, ac mae Cymru mewn safle arbennig o dda i elwa yn economaidd o hynny am genedlaethau i ddod.

contributions.text_english: Thank you very much, Ministers.
contributions.text_original: Diolch yn fawr iawn ichi, Weinidogion.

contributions.text_english: We will now move on to item 2, questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language. The first question is from Becca Martin.
contributions.text_original: Symudwn ymlaen i eitem 2, cwestiynau i'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Addysg a'r Gymraeg. Cwestiwn 1, Becca Martin.

contributions.text_english: 1. Will the Cabinet Minister ensure that adults who wish to learn Welsh have access to more opportunities to develop their language skills? OQ64524
contributions.text_original: 1. A wnaiff y Gweinidog Cabinet sicrhau bod oedolion sy'n dymuno dysgu Cymraeg yn cael mynediad at fwy o gyfleoedd i ddatblygu eu sgiliau iaith? OQ64524

contributions.text_english: Thank you very much for the question. The good news is that more people are learning Welsh than ever before, and it's wonderful to see interest growing amongst people of all ages and of all backgrounds. The Welsh Government is investing over £18 million in the National Centre for Learning Welsh this year to create opportunities for adults and young people to learn Welsh. The centre provides online provision, face-to-face provision and hybrid provision across all levels to its learners.
contributions.text_original: Diolch yn fawr iawn am y cwestiwn. Y newyddion da yw bod mwy o bobl yn dysgu Cymraeg nag erioed o'r blaen, ac mae'n braf gweld diddordeb yn tyfu ymysg pobl o bob oedran ac o bob cefndir. Mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn buddsoddi dros £18 miliwn yn y Ganolfan Dysgu Cymraeg Genedlaethol eleni i greu cyfleoedd i oedolion a phobl ifanc i ddysgu'r iaith. Mae'r ganolfan yn cynnig darpariaeth ar-lein, wyneb yn wyneb neu hybrid ar draws pob lefel i'w dysgwyr.

contributions.text_english: Diolch. It's widely accepted that one of the most effective ways for a child to learn the Welsh language, or any language, is through immersion. Simply put, the more Welsh a child hears and uses, the more likely they are to develop the language effectively. The trochi method, or immersion, can also foster a deeper understanding of, and a connection to, Welsh culture and history. However, for too many children, this immersion stops at the school gates. Many children come from English-speaking homes, which is the case in my home, and may have limited opportunities to hear or use Welsh within their wider communities. This is particularly prevalent in north-east Wales, where I am an elected representative. I'm regularly told that the issue is not a lack of desire to learn Welsh, but a lack of opportunities for adults to develop their language skills to a conversational standard. Will the Minister work with partner organisations and external agencies to provide additional opportunities for adult learners to use the language they have, helping to create stronger Welsh-speaking communities and in turn support the next generation of Welsh speakers?
contributions.text_original: Diolch. It's widely accepted that one of the most effective ways for a child to learn the Welsh language, or any language, is through immersion. Simply put, the more Welsh a child hears and uses, the more likely they are to develop the language effectively. The trochi method, or immersion, can also foster a deeper understanding of, and a connection to, Welsh culture and history. However, for too many children, this immersion stops at the school gates. Many children come from English-speaking homes, which is the case in my home, and may have limited opportunities to hear or use Welsh within their wider communities. This is particularly prevalent in north-east Wales, where I am an elected representative. I'm regularly told that the issue is not a lack of desire to learn Welsh, but a lack of opportunities for adults to develop their language skills to a conversational standard. Will the Minister work with partner organisations and external agencies to provide additional opportunities for adult learners to use the language they have, helping to create stronger Welsh-speaking communities and in turn support the next generation of Welsh speakers?

Diolch yn fawr iawn. Thank you very much indeed. Immersion teaching has been with us in Wales for many years, and it's the proven way of ensuring that children acquire the Welsh language, the target language, in the most effective way possible. This was based on work that was done in Canada, where they have immersion programmes. We know that children from non-Welsh-speaking backgrounds acquire the Welsh language fluently through immersion schools. But what we need as well is support for the parents, like yourself, who are learning with their children. I know the national language centre does provide funding and support for parents through various programmes, so that they can learn with their children at the pace their children are developing.

This is equally important in terms of helping parents to help their children with homework, which is one of the barriers that many parents have about putting their children into Welsh-medium schools: 'How can I help with homework?' I can provide many answers to that. First, it's not their parents' homework anyway, but I could go on and on. But where they feel that they can help, learning Welsh is important and helps develop a bond between parents and their children through that second language. I think that sends a positive signal to families about the importance of bilingualism and living in a bilingual Wales.

contributions.text_english: As a Welsh language learner, I'm delighted to have the opportunity to learn Welsh in the Senedd.
contributions.text_original: As a Welsh language learner, I'm delighted to have the opportunity to learn Welsh in the Senedd.

contributions.text_english: I'm Sarah Edwards, and I'm learning Welsh.
contributions.text_original: Sarah Edwards ydw i, a dwi'n dysgu Cymraeg.

contributions.text_english: Can the Cabinet Minister comment on what provisions are being set out by the Welsh Government to upgrade Welsh language learning facilities in my own constituency of rural Carmarthenshire? Diolch.
contributions.text_original: Can the Cabinet Minister comment on what provisions are being set out by the Welsh Government to upgrade Welsh language learning facilities in my own constituency of rural Carmarthenshire? Diolch.

contributions.text_english: Congratulations for learning Welsh. You live, like I do, in a county where the Welsh language is an important part of the community.
contributions.text_original: Llongyfarchiadau mawr am ddysgu Cymraeg. Rŷch chi'n byw, fel fi, mewn sir lle mae'r Gymraeg yn rhan bwysig o'r gymuned.

contributions.text_english:
Carmarthenshire, which we share in terms of our constituency, is a predominantly Welsh-speaking area, and it is great that people like you are learning the language. The national centre that I referred to earlier on provides funding, and the Welsh Government gives them £18 million to provide funding for courses that are tailored to the needs of people, whether that is in the community, in the Senedd, in workplaces, and online as well. As a former Welsh language tutor myself, I know how important it is for those courses to be available in workplaces in particular, but also in the community.

The joy of the workplace is that a place like the Senedd does give you opportunities not only to learn the language, but to use the language as well, as you have effectively done this afternoon. I would encourage all Members and all staff members in the Senedd, and other workplaces across Wales, to learn the language and be supported in a sensitive and effective way by those of us who are Welsh speakers by engaging with you and practising the language with you. Because learning Welsh is a virtuous cycle in many different ways. It's to do with confidence, it's to do with opportunity and it's to do with developing skills. That cycle needs to be continued and developed until you become fluent to use the language in all kinds of different ways in life. Da iawn.
contributions.text_original:
Carmarthenshire, which we share in terms of our constituency, is a predominantly Welsh-speaking area, and it is great that people like you are learning the language. The national centre that I referred to earlier on provides funding, and the Welsh Government gives them £18 million to provide funding for courses that are tailored to the needs of people, whether that is in the community, in the Senedd, in workplaces, and online as well. As a former Welsh language tutor myself, I know how important it is for those courses to be available in workplaces in particular, but also in the community.

The joy of the workplace is that a place like the Senedd does give you opportunities not only to learn the language, but to use the language as well, as you have effectively done this afternoon. I would encourage all Members and all staff members in the Senedd, and other workplaces across Wales, to learn the language and be supported in a sensitive and effective way by those of us who are Welsh speakers by engaging with you and practising the language with you. Because learning Welsh is a virtuous cycle in many different ways. It's to do with confidence, it's to do with opportunity and it's to do with developing skills. That cycle needs to be continued and developed until you become fluent to use the language in all kinds of different ways in life. Da iawn.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you, Deputy Presiding Officer. Cabinet Minister, let's just have a little look back over 20 years of the Programme for International Student Assessment in Wales. Back in 2006, Jane Hutt:

'we can learn from the best and most effective practice'.

We move on to Leighton Andrews, who, to his credit, had a bit of a crack at this, quite forthright. He talked about 'systemic failure'. A few more years to Huw Lewis—'no quick fixes'. Kirsty Williams, who was in post for quite a while:

'it will take time for Welsh education reforms to be reflected in PISA results'.

Well, a Liberal did get one prediction correct there. Jeremy Miles:

'a renewed national focus on reading, numeracy and science'. 

And then, obviously, a few years later, yourself:

'not where we want them'.

I should say, during that period, I actually was partly responsible for administering PISA in a couple of schools in Wales, so I know a little bit about it. It's a grim tale, Minister. It feels like groundhog day for the younger Members. Perhaps that's a film well worth watching. We feel stuck in a loop. My question is: why should we think that this Welsh Government's announcements will make any difference?

Thank you for the gallop through PISA in Wales that I think most of us are familiar with and has got us to a place where we don't want to be. What is different about this plan is its focus on nought to 16 as the first element in that. We recognise that the very earliest years have an impact on learners' development in schools. We're tying it in very firmly with all the interventions that we are making in that space, in order that we can apply the support for those learners and for staff that is appropriate. I'm also—and this too is new—looking at a baseline for entry into schools, a year 6 indicator, which I and others will be able to be held to account for the trajectory we are making in literacy and numeracy, and we also want to see improvements in qualifications outcomes at 16.

What I am keen to do is to make live in our schools system the ability to demonstrate what we are doing, what you can hold me to account on, and the clarity that we give school staff about those expectations. The plan will be published in detail for consultation, in terms of what those expectations look like, very soon. And we will be able to see, on literacy and numeracy specifically, in which direction we are going, and that is different from the responses in the past.

Thank you, Cabinet Secretary. I hear what you're saying, but there's nothing new in baseline assessment. Perhaps it'll be different from what we've had previously. [Interruption.] Yes. I mean, we can go back to 1998, and there was the literacy and numeracy framework, which never got adopted—didn't see its way through devolution.

Putting that to one side, I'm going to talk about the Curriculum for Wales, because the Curriculum for Wales will be cited as having the potential to improve pupil outcomes. But last week, the Scottish Government announced its largest ever review of the curriculum up there in over 15 years, because of their poor PISA results. And unfortunately, for those who don't know, the Curriculum for Wales was largely based, not exclusively, but largely based on their Curriculum for Excellence in Scotland, as it was called. Its DNA runs right through our curriculum here. I describe it as the mashed potato of the curriculum—it's bland and of little nutritious value.

Minister, since we've not yet seen the impact of the new curriculum on PISA results, and Scotland has, my fear is that matters are going to get worse, and potentially a lot worse. Will you follow the lead of Scotland and announce your own review of the Welsh school curriculum?

Okay. Finally, you touched on qualifications at 16—I'm just going to touch on those at 18. There are those who believe that PISA results are stand-alone and don't contribute to anything in particular, because we've got GCSE and A-level results. Let's just look at A-level results, because you can't really compare them to England any longer, because both GCSEs and A-levels, whilst they're branded the same, have not got the same structure, and have not necessarily got the same gradings either.

But we do have comparative data for university entry, and I'm just going to focus on Cambridge University. This is not the complete picture, but when we look at some of the data published by Cambridge University, going back over a decade, a few things come to light. During the last three years, there were 325 applicants from Wales to Cambridge, and 21 per cent of those were ultimately successful. If we roll back a decade, we're at 260 applicants, so fewer applicants, but 30 per cent were successful. And I should point out the success rate for Scotland last year was just 12 per cent, and that's a real worry, because we've adopted that curriculum. It's the trend that matters—there are more applying, but fewer are successful.

My question to you, Minister, is: would you commission—because I've only had a snapshot there—some independent research to see whether fewer students from Wales are successful in their applications to the competitive universities and the competitive courses?

There are two points there to take up, I think. Looking at the trajectory and progression of students into post-18 and post-16 education is part, I think, of my colleague's review, and that will feature in that regard.

I think, on GCSEs and A-levels, it is important to remember that none of the pupils, the learners, who have done Curriculum for Wales have yet gone through these qualifications. So, drawing lessons about Curriculum for Wales with these particular cohorts may not be as helpful as we need at this point.

I think, also, it's important to remember that the consistency of testing—. PISA is one test and it tells us valuable things, and I want to draw on the detail and the granular detail of what that tells us, particularly how good we are at stretching our most able learners. I want to look at that and feed that knowledge and information into our plan. What is also clear, though, is that it doesn't measure everything. GCSEs measure something slightly different. A-levels, in which we perform, actually, very well, measure something else. So, I think it is important and is a responsibility to think of all these results in the round, while also being clear about what our expectations are, particularly around foundational skills, which is what our plan is about.

You'll be aware, in my own constituency, that Flintshire council has proposed the merger of four schools into one superschool, with communities at the periphery of that, such as in Saltney, with St Anthony's school, and in Mold, with St David's school—where my colleague Darren Millar is the Member for—particularly concerned about the impact from the distance of the site that's being proposed.

The point here, Cabinet Minister, is that the consultation for the proposal has been rejected by more than 96 per cent of respondents. Schools are at the heart of our communities, and their closures have a particularly stark impact on rural areas, where schools serve as important community buildings and set habits of a lifetime for travel to and from school. Councils should not be imposing school closures on communities that do not want them. Instead, closures should only be considered where there's significant evidence, considerable public support and action to mitigate impacts on those communities. So, within the powers that you do have, Cabinet Minister, will you commit today to supporting parents, teachers and learners in disputes over school closures?

contributions.text_english: Minister, it's vitally important that Wales's unique culture is not only preserved but nurtured. Access to Welsh-medium education for those who want it will be an important part of that process. More than that, bilingualism is literally good for the brain. It leads to better executive function, better memory, problem solving, and even delays dementia onset by an average of around five years. Of course, Wales isn't the only country that recognises the importance of language in the transmission of culture. There are examples that we can learn from from across the globe. I'd be interested to know if the Welsh Government has learned or is trying to learn anything from Catalonia and the Basque region in successfully promoting bilingualism.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you, Cabinet Minister. We can't ignore the clear link between social deprivation, child poverty and educational attainment, which I think are all areas that successive Governments have failed to address. The latest PISA results should be a wake-up call for this Government. Wales is bottom of the UK in maths, reading and science. Maths has fallen significantly, and your own Government acknowledges that Wales has constantly lagged behind other UK nations. But nowhere should that failure concern us more than in communities such as the one I represent in Pontypridd Cynon Merthyr. Your own deprivation figures show that 83 per cent of areas in Merthyr Tydfil are among the most educationally deprived areas of Wales. So, Cabinet Minister, those statistics aren't just something to read on a Government spreadsheet; they represent children whose future opportunities depend upon the education they receive today.

Now, I appreciate the PISA records aren't yours to own, as they're based on 2025 results, and Labour spent years reforming the curriculum, changing qualifications and moving away. However, it's not lost on anyone on this side of the Chamber that Plaid Cymru supported that, so you can no longer blame the system you inherited. So, the question is: do you commit to working across Government departments to ensure that socially deprived areas in Wales are prioritised to make sure that we close the gap between those and any educational achievements for PISA? Thank you.

Diolch yn fawr. Spending time litigating previous Governments' records is not how I intend to use my time, because I want to move forward from here, so I have no intention of starting today. I think you will see a commitment across this Government particularly to tackle the impact of poverty on children across Wales, both in schools and more broadly in our society. That's why the childcare offer, for example, is such a focus for us. You will see, in each of our portfolios, I think, a strategic commitment to tackling the impact of poverty in Wales on children and on societies and on families across our country, including in your constituency.

You will see also, in the foundational literacy and numeracy plan that I published last week, that there is in that explicitly a commitment to looking at our success in delivering this plan in terms of how well we are getting to grips with those gaps, because some of these statistics are alarmingly and stubbornly high and have been for a very long time. And I hope you will have heard, over the past few weeks, how important that is, in all its complexity, for all of us.

contributions.text_english: Welsh-medium education succeeds when every child learns in the way that's appropriate to them as individuals, of course. I have a grandson who's living with autism. He's in a Welsh-medium school and he's getting excellent support, I have to say—it's excellent and I'm very grateful for that. Unfortunately, not every family is in that same situation, because this isn't true across other areas in Wales. Having additional learning needs shouldn't mean that learners have to give up their right to Welsh-medium education. Every child and young person, whatever their needs, should be able to access the support and provision that they need through the medium of Welsh. So, will the Cabinet Minister provide an update on the Welsh Government's plans to ensure that additional learning needs provision through the medium of Welsh is just as accessible, inclusive and effective as the provision through the medium of English?

contributions.text_english:
Well, Deputy Minister, it is, of course, Adult Learners Week this week, and I was really grateful to the adult learners who met me in Coleg y Cymoedd in Aberdare on Monday, who spoke about their experiences of re-entering education.

We know that there's considerable demand for adult education, but figures that I've seen from Adult Learning Wales suggest that demand in 2026-27 outstrips their funding by almost 10 percent, and that means that around 850 potential learners are missing out. I'm told by Adult Learning Wales that they could put additional funding to use immediately, upskilling workers and allowing for more flexible delivery. So, how is Welsh Government making meeting this demand a priority?

Well, again, you make a really important point. Let me just agree with you that, with adult learning, the benefits are so wide-ranging. It supports the development of skills, improves health and well-being and is a catalyst for social engagement and integration. It also shows that well-paid work, through developing skills, is the best route out of poverty, and helping people to gain the skills they need to thrive and work is a clear priority for this Welsh Government. And I'm looking forward to the awards ceremony this evening as well, the Inspire! adult learning awards. It is, for me—and I've been to many over recent years—one of the highlights of the year, when you see the outstanding achievements of learners whose passion, commitment and dedication I think demonstrates the transformative power of lifelong learning.

And I'm aware that Medr have given £6.25 million in this financial year, which straddles half the academic year, to help FE colleges, but we are monitoring the situation with Medr, and, if funding allows, we will try and support the FE sector but also adult learning in general as best as we can.

contributions.text_english:
A high number of schools across my constituency of Caerdydd Ffynnon Taf are facing a maintenance backlog. Scaffolding has surrounded Roath Park primary since 2021, Marlborough Road primary since 2022 and Albany primary since 2023. The condition of a number of comprehensives is substandard and very close to being further downgraded, including the second-hand Welsh-medium comprehensives ysgol Bro Edern and ysgol Plasmawr.

Most worryingly, parents at Albany Primary School were advised the week before this term started that their children would be sent out to three different schools because of dry rot. This late notice was despite Estyn warning in October 2025 that the site management arrangements at Albany Primary School, and I quote,

'give cause for concern and have been brought to the attention of the local authority.'

What discussions has the Cabinet Minister had with Cardiff Council regarding the condition of their school estate, and the council's response to Estyn in particular, and whether earlier intervention could have avoided Albany primary's closure and the severe disruption caused to pupils' education?

Diolch, Minister, for your answer. Just three months into this financial year, Swansea Council has already overspent by £13.7 million over its budget. contributions.text_english: The Senedd Commission is committed to ensuring that we are inclusive to everyone who works on or visits the estate. We have facilities available for those who need to express milk following the birth of their child. The quiet rooms can be used for expressing milk, and fridges are available to store the milk. These can be found on the ground floor in Tŷ Hywel in B block, opposite the committee rooms, and one in the Senedd on the Neuadd level. In addition, people can access the first aid rooms, where privacy, seating or couch facilities are provided. All these facilities are lockable and can be marked as occupied. For Commission staff, managers and HR support return-to-work planning after maternity leave in a number of ways, including a new and expectant parent risk assessment, covering practical arrangements such as quiet rooms, hygiene facilities and secure refrigerated storage.

I was initially offered the medical room you mentioned, but it only had a bed in it, and you can't pump lying down, and I do need a desk and chair to work, and I couldn't possibly lose two hours of my working day. So, I was wondering if you would look at creating a space for pumping that enables people to work at the same time, and confirm to me that no member of staff or Member will face the same circumstances I was in.

contributions.text_english: Diolch, Joe. Bay 32 is the Commission’s project to secure fit-for-purpose accommodation beyond the expiry of the Tŷ Hywel lease, which happens in 2032. A competitive procurement concluded that the best value option is a major refurbishment and renewal of Tŷ Hywel, with the potential for Commission ownership. Equitix is the preferred bidder and its proposal includes more than £50 million of landlord investment—landlord investment—in the building. This is planned to include increasing the amount of useable space in Tŷ Hywel by 25 per cent. The project is now in detailed design during a pre-development phase with capped costs to the Commission. Because the building must remain operational during major works, temporary accommodation will be needed for Members, staff and for services. So, the Commission will consider options for managing any relocation, before considering the full business case later this year. The works are currently expected to begin from early summer 2027 and last for up to three years.

contributions.text_original: 3. Pa asesiad y mae'r Comisiwn wedi'i wneud o effaith yr ôl-groniad parhaus o daliadau o Gynllun Pensiwn y Gwasanaeth Sifil ar ei gyflogeion presennol a chyn-gyflogeion? OQ64546

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Lindsay. Responsibility for administering the civil service pension scheme transferred from MyCSP to Capita on 1 December 2025. The change was intended to modernise the service, but the transfer included a substantial volume of cases affecting some retirement quotations and new pension payments. The Cabinet Office and Capita established a recovery programme to prioritise urgent and hardship cases, clear outstanding work, and restore contracted service standards.

The Commission currently has fewer than five former employees who have retired since Capita became the administrators, one of which has accessed the hardship loan scheme introduced by the Commission, in line with Cabinet Office guidance, to mitigate the financial impact, and we continue to monitor the situation and seek assurances that outstanding cases are resolved very quickly.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Francesca. The Commission takes the welfare of Members and their staff very seriously, and we provide practical, accessible support across well-being, employment, health and safety, dignity and respect, safeguarding, and, of course, security. This includes confidential employee assistance and occupational health services, tailored HR guidance and training, and security advice and measures. The Hwb brings information and face-to-face support together in one place, with a weekly virtual drop-in for support staff, whatever their location.

The Commission's phased learning framework treats personal resilience, well-being and maintaining a healthy work-life balance as continuing development needs rather than one-off induction topics. Training is repeated, reinforced and extended through the Senedd term, with provision adapted to Member and support staff learning needs and delivery preferences. 

And just finally, the Members' security team provides support to Members on a wide range of personal safety and security matters, including advice and guidance, the implementation of security measures at homes and offices, practical support and advice relating to social media security, and the reporting and management of security-related incidents.

contributions.text_english: Diolch for the description there. If I can provide some context to my question, and the scene I want to picture: Members of this Chamber and their support staff come into the Tŷ Hywel building each day to carry out their work freely, often in areas where members of the public are excluded unless they're chaperoned around the building. However, what's become quite clear is that we do have journalists, dare I say, lurking along the corridors in areas that we don't know. Some could be on the radio. We don't know who they are, or what they look like. I can give an example of that, if I may: just before the summer recess, going into the ladies' bathroom on level 2 and meeting a very chatty lady as I came out of the cubicle—and I know we all like a good chat, and I'm one for those—however, she asked for my number, when I believed perhaps she was support staff for one of my colleagues, and it was actually a journalist. So, I do think there are lines being blurred here between the access that they have to our workspace and kind of being led down a garden path, shall I say? I don't think that's appropriate, and I do wonder whether we can consider that they are put in a certain restricted area and not have free access to where we work, including the bathrooms as well.
