contributions.text_english: I thank the Member for raising this important point. I hope that the Member and also everyone else in this Senedd agrees with me that we also, as Members of the Senedd, must take responsibility for looking after each other, whatever our party. This is especially important when the online world is becoming ever more violent towards politicians, especially young women. Therefore, as I speak about the online world, I'd like to ask what the Commission is doing to support Members of the Senedd and staff who see their well-being being negatively impacted because of the increase that we have all seen in online abuse, especially with AI as well, and deepfakes, just as an example for you.
contributions.text_original: Diolch i'r Aelod am godi'r cwestiwn pwysig yma. Dwi'n gobeithio bod yr Aelod a hefyd pawb arall yn y Senedd yma'n cytuno â fi bod yn rhaid i ni hefyd fel Aelodau o'r Senedd gymryd cyfrifoldeb i edrych ar ôl ein gilydd, pa bynnag blaid. Mae hyn yn enwedig o bwysig pan mae'r byd ar-lein yn dod yn fwy treisgar tuag at wleidyddion, yn enwedig menywod ifanc. Felly, wrth i fi siarad am y byd ar-lein, hoffwn wybod beth mae'r Comisiwn yn ei wneud er mwyn cefnogi Aelodau o'r Senedd a staff sydd yn gweld eu lles yn cael ei effeithio'n negyddol oherwydd y cynnydd rydyn ni i gyd wedi gweld mewn cam-drin ar-lein, yn enwedig gydag AI hefyd, a deepfakes, jest fel enghraifft i ti.

contributions.text_english: Diolch yn fawr iawn. I would refer Members very strongly not just to the Hwb, but to the security team presence as well, for all the advice and assistance they can give. Of course, there is an interaction that we have, not just as individual Members, but through our security people, including the observation and monitoring. It's not monitoring in a NASA style, but keeping an eye on what's happening online. There is engagement as well with police across Wales. This is an issue that affects all Members, because it can be quite a hostile environment out there. But I would strongly say to Members and their staff that if they have individual instances, they should bring them to the attention of our security people, because they want to hear about it and we need to be notified of it.

contributions.text_english: 8. What safeguarding checks does the Commission require of Members of the Senedd before they undertake activities involving children and young people? OQ64547
contributions.text_original: 8. Pa wiriadau diogelu y mae'r Comisiwn yn gofyn i Aelodau o'r Senedd eu gwneud cyn iddynt ymgymryd â gweithgareddau sy'n ymwneud â phlant a phobl ifanc? OQ64547

contributions.text_english: Diolch, Jane. Responsibility for safeguarding arrangements within Members' offices rests with the individual Members, as Members of the Senedd are individually elected and they're not Commission employees. Members need to have their own safeguarding policy appropriate to their role as office holders and employers, as they are responsible for their activities. The statutory disclosure and barring framework is reserved to the UK level.

contributions.text_english: During my first term as a Senedd Member, I was really surprised that I could go into any school, any youth club, any provision where a child, a young person or a vulnerable person lived or worked without any checks, without any need to show any documentation. On all of those visits, I was accompanied by somebody, but it wouldn't take a genius and it wouldn't take much imagination for somebody quite powerful, who is a Member of the Senedd, to say, 'I'd like to do this on my own'. I do believe it is the Senedd's responsibility to ensure that Senedd Members, who have access and are in powerful roles to influence other people—. It should take the responsibility. There is no reference to this in any recent documentation, and I raised it in the last Senedd. I wonder if the Senedd Commission could take this forward, even on a voluntary basis, to look at how Members could get a DBS check, which doesn't give you an absolute safety mark, but it is a tool in the toolbox that ensures that this Parliament is not putting children, young people and vulnerable people at risk by allowing Senedd Members to do their duties. Diolch yn fawr iawn.

contributions.text_english: Thank you. There are a couple of points for consideration here. First of all, the statutory disclosure and barring framework is reserved to UK level, so broadening eligibility for things such as enhanced checks would require action by the UK Government. I'm aware that political parties operate, on a voluntary basis, their own approach to candidates, and it differs from party to party. We watch with interest the different proposals that are emerging currently at a UK level from some individual MPs. Some of them are looking at a statutory basis for changing this, and some at a non-statutory basis. The basic test, as you mentioned, in terms of DBS, as opposed to the enhanced test, has some limitations with it in terms of what it provides. My understanding is that DBS checks are legally designed as a tool for employers or for licensing bodies to assess the suitability of an applicant for a specific workplace role. MSs, of course, not unlike MPs, are not employees, but independent constitutional office holders chosen directly by voters. But it is an interesting area, and we're watching the discussions going on in Westminster at the moment. But the responsibility rests with UK statute.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you for that answer. I think we've been here before, haven't we? When the Commission considered this issue in July, it argued that Sky News alone provided proficient plurality on the Senedd's television system. I would respectfully suggest that, in the time since GB News was removed from the Senedd's system, the media landscape has changed. Since the departure of Laurence Fox, GB News has continued to grow its audience and broaden its reach. It now reaches over 1 million viewers per day and, in 2025, overtook Sky News as the UK's largest commercial news channel by average viewing figures.

Whether Members agree with GB News or not is beside the point. It is an Ofcom-regulated broadcaster watched by millions of people across the United Kingdom. I'm sure that everybody on this side of the Chamber is a fan of GB News. Excluding it from the Senedd's internal television system risks creating the impression that some lawful viewpoints are more acceptable than others. In the interests of pluralism, free expression and informed democratic debate, will the Commission now review its policy and reconsider the inclusion of GB News on the Senedd estate? Diolch.

contributions.text_english: Diolch, Gwyn. Ease of access to the existing routes from Tŷ Hywel to the Senedd building, and significant improvements to how the buildings connect for Members and other users, is actively being looked at in detail as part of the Bay 32 project. The Commission is not, however, currently considering any further alternative physical bridges, for example, to the Senedd building from Tŷ Hywel. There are two link bridges that provide access from Tŷ Hywel to the Senedd building—one via the first floor staff restaurant and one on the second floor. Access from the first floor link bridge is via lifts only. The second floor link bridge directly joins the Senedd building, with no lift required. Direct access is also available at ground floor level via the Senedd building courtyards.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch. This week is Adult Learners' Week, and I'd like to pay tribute to all the adult learners across Wales. It's sometimes difficult to step back into education, so it's so important that there's support there for them. The impact of adult learning is life-changing, and extends far beyond education. It improves health and well-being, and is fundamental to Wales's economic growth. It enables adults to access upskilling and reskilling and enhance their lives in ways that we will never understand. 

The adult community learning programme in particular offers people an important route into education, supporting people to access learning in a setting and at a pace that is right for them. Tonight, the Inspire! adult learning awards are going to take place, and I'd like to congratulate Hannah from my constituency in Caerdydd Penarth who will be receiving the new Welsh speaker award. 

Hannah will be recognised alongside 10 other award winners who are all being celebrated for their commitment, dedication and achievements—learners who have changed their lives through adult education. I hope these stories, and thousands like them across Wales, can encourage more people to embrace the message of Adult Learners' Week—to never stop learning. Diolch.

Diolch. This week is Adult Learners' Week, and I'd like to pay tribute to all the adult learners across Wales. It's sometimes difficult to step back into education, so it's so important that there's support there for them. The impact of adult learning is life-changing, and extends far beyond education. It improves health and well-being, and is fundamental to Wales's economic growth. It enables adults to access upskilling and reskilling and enhance their lives in ways that we will never understand. 

The adult community learning programme in particular offers people an important route into education, supporting people to access learning in a setting and at a pace that is right for them. Tonight, the Inspire! adult learning awards are going to take place, and I'd like to congratulate Hannah from my constituency in Caerdydd Penarth who will be receiving the new Welsh speaker award. 

Hannah will be recognised alongside 10 other award winners who are all being celebrated for their commitment, dedication and achievements—learners who have changed their lives through adult education. I hope these stories, and thousands like them across Wales, can encourage more people to embrace the message of Adult Learners' Week—to never stop learning. Diolch.

Last Friday marked International Equal Pay Day, a UN awareness day of gender inequality and the gender pay gap between men and women. Sadly, this is a pressing issue for Wales. The latest state of the nation report on gender equality by the Women's Equality Network Wales exposed that the gender pay gap in Wales has widened to 9.7 per cent. On average, female employees earn £15.78 per hour, whilst male employees earn £17.48. Compared to men, women are over three times more likely to be out of the job market due to caring responsibilities. Women are also three times more likely to work part-time, which is limiting to earnings and progression. And women are more likely to work in sectors and roles that are lower paid, such as health and social care. We need change. 

Barriers to economic equality, like unequal caring responsibilities and gender stereotypes, must be challenged. Women must be supported to access better paid jobs, skills and training programmes throughout their careers, and we must have robust and inclusive policies on flexible working, harassment, menopause and parental leave. This International Equal Pay Day, I urge all colleagues across the Senedd to champion gender equality and help create a Wales free from gender discrimination. Diolch yn fawr.

Next month, Wyeside Arts Centre in Builth Wells celebrates an incredible milestone—50 years of bringing arts and culture to the heart of rural mid Wales. The fiftieth birthday weekend brings that history to life, with Welsh music, poetry, art and community participation. At its centre is Cymuned Gwy, a new bilingual work commissioned for the anniversary, inspired by the River Wye and the people who live alongside it. Wyeside is a small, independent charity, but its contribution is anything but small. Open six days a week, it provides cinema, live performance, music, exhibitions and opportunities for people to come together across a large rural area. 

Places like Wyeside offer far more than entertainment. They are places where people meet, participate and belong. The anniversary, as well as looking forward and back, has amazing plans to introduce to people as well, which will improve accessibility, and new facilities that will serve mid Wales for decades to come. Alongside this celebration, we know there is a serious challenge. Despite operating all year round, generating much of its income, and being supported by a small team of volunteers, Wyeside continues to face a significant revenue shortfall. I congratulate everyone who has sustained Wyeside over 50 years, and encourage colleagues to join the celebrations from 9 to 11 October, to see its plans for the future, and help ensure it remains at the heart of mid Wales. Diolch yn fawr iawn.

It's Migraine Awareness Week, and I want to recognise people across Wales living with a condition that is too often dismissed. Migraines affect one in seven people in the UK. It's a neurological condition that can cause severe pain, sickness and sensitivity to light and sound. Its impact reaches far beyond an attack. It affects work, family life and mental well-being. 

The Migraine Trust's latest survey found that nine in 10 respondents had felt disbelief about the severity or the impact of their migraine. Nearly a third had experienced this from their colleagues or their managers. More than three quarters say that the disbelief has damaged their mental health. Nobody should have to fight to be believed while already struggling with pain. The trust's 'Believe me' campaign carries a simple message to us all: listen, take migraine seriously and offer practical support. To people living with migraine in Gŵyr Abertawe, and across Wales: your experience matters. Pain does not have to be visible to deserve understanding, and a little patience and compassion can make a difference. Diolch.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Lywydd. Can I draw Members' attention to my register of interests and the fact that I'm an adult learner in Cardiff and Vale College?

Today, I want to focus on one of Wales's greatest success stories and one that too often does not receive the recognition it deserves: our further education colleges. Across Wales, colleges are changing lives every day. For young people, they are the chance to take that first step after school and progress to work, an apprenticeship or to university. For adults, they are access to lifelong learning, and for employers, they are the support they need to upskill their workforce, improve productivity and compete for new business.

Across Wales, colleges have shown that they are innovators and are ready to meet new challenges. In north Wales, they are helping to drive the new tertiary alliance with our university sector. In south-west Wales, the four colleges have come together to form a new partnership to maximise opportunities from the Celtic Freeport. And in south-east Wales, colleges have pioneered new ways of supporting learners, including the junior apprenticeship programme I was so proud to support in Government. The evidence of their value is clear.

This year, colleges across Wales have seen record levels of demand, with every college reporting increased participation. More learners than ever are choosing further education as their route into skills, qualifications and careers. Demand is particularly strong in vocational and technical subjects, such as construction, engineering and health and care—precisely the sectors we know are critical to Wales's future prosperity. Colleges are also providing opportunities for those who need them most. They are supporting thousands of learners who are returning to education, improving literacy and numeracy and rebuilding confidence after difficult experiences in school or elsewhere.

This is a Welsh success story, but it is fragile, and more learners means more pressure on space and on budgets. And the pressures are urgent, with ColegauCymru estimating the sector will have enrolled a record 50,000 young people this academic year. At a time when we are in the middle of a crisis with the number of young people who are not in employment, education or training, and when we are weeks away from the publication of the Milburn review, there has never been a more important time to invest in further education.

So, rising participation is a good news story. It is a sign that colleges are succeeding, it is a sign that further education is delivering for Wales and it is an opportunity for Wales. However, record demand brings with it a significant challenge. We know that funding has not kept pace with participation. Last year, I was able to put an additional £20 million in to support participation in the sector, but this year, the shortfall is estimated by both the sector and by Medr to be around £23.5 million. To stop even more learners missing out on places, colleges have been forced to make the difficult choice of moving funding from adult part-time provision to pay for full-time learner numbers. This all means there are around 5,000 learners who are studying for whom the sector isn't receiving any funding. Hundreds of learners have not got a place at all, and hundreds more did not get their first-choice course because of a shortage of places.

As well as pressure on places, it is also stretching vital support, such as well-being services, mental health support, financial hardship provision and learner travel. I hope Members know my own personal commitment to supporting learners with additional learning needs, and I am concerned about the impact of underfunding. Early data from ColegauCymru suggests an additional 65 per cent increase in learners with individual development plans, and it is essential that they can access the funding they need.

Looking ahead, the pressures in 2027-28 are even greater. The sector estimates that at least £40 million will be required in the 2027-28 academic year simply to maintain existing participation levels and respond to sustained learner demand. Pay and other inflationary pressures will push this even higher. If that funding is not available, the consequences could be significant. We risk more young people becoming disconnected from education and training. We risk job losses in the sector and cuts to support services. We risk cutting progression routes to our universities and stopping young people from taking that first step on their career paths. And we risk cutting off the skills pipeline that businesses need to compete and grow.

That is why this motion is important. It calls for a clear assessment of the consequences of failing to fund increased participation in further education. We need to understand the impact on learner pathways, on not in education, employment or training levels, on staff, on learner support services, and on progression into employment and higher education. Further education colleges take a much greater proportion of learners from lower income backgrounds. It is vital that we understand the impact on deprived communities across Wales. For many young people, particularly those with the fewest qualifications, college is their second chance, and they have very few options if they don't get a place. We owe it to the young people and to the adults who rely on further education to ensure our colleges have the resources they need.

Llywydd, this debate is ultimately about opportunity. When people want to learn, train and improve their prospects, our response should not be to limit opportunity, our response should be to understand the consequences of inaction and ensure that Wales continues to invest in success. Our colleges have demonstrated their value. They are helping young people realise their potential, supporting employers and strengthening communities across Wales. Now we must ensure that the resources available to them reflect the vital role they play. I urge Members to support our motion. Diolch.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Lywydd. I move the amendment in the name of my colleague Paul Davies. I'd like to thank Labour colleagues for bringing this debate forward today; a really important issue has been highlighted in this Chamber. I certainly support the opening remarks by their spokesperson here this afternoon. We know, don't we, that the latest Welsh Government figures show that 17 per cent of 16 to 24-year-olds in Wales were not in employment, education or training in the year ending December 2025. That's an increase of 5.5 percentage points in just one year. That's nearly one in every five young adults that we would meet not in education, employment or training. Quite stark figures. Sometimes, Llywydd, we get so used to these numbers being bandied about, but it's pretty shocking, actually, that nearly one in five young adults are not in education, training or in employment.

We must remember that behind every one of those numbers is a young person who wants to get on with their life, to continue education, develop their skills, or step into the world of work. When they're unable to do so, as this motion recognises, the consequences can be long-lasting, affecting their health, earnings, life chances and ultimately affecting our society as a whole. That's why the role that further education colleges play in tackling this is so, so important. I know the Welsh Government do understand this, but what we need to see today as a result of this motion is action off the back of words.

We know, of course, that record numbers of learners are choosing further education colleges as a route into qualifications, skills and careers, with every college in Wales reporting an increase in participation this academic year. Minister, you'll be pleased to hear, of course, that I visited a college on Friday just gone. It was Coleg Cambria's Yale site in Wrexham. They had me playing pickleball in one of their sports halls, they had me observing some pickle being prepared in the restaurant, and I hope to God that there's no footage of me getting in a pickle on the dance floor in their dance studio.

What they told me about also was the increased demand that they're seeing at their own site there in Wrexham, which I know reflects colleges across Wales experiencing the same kinds of pressures. We know that there's particularly a strong demand in vocational and technical education areas, such as construction, engineering and healthcare, which happen to be precisely the sectors where Wales needs skilled workers today. And as we've already heard in the opening remarks, Llywydd, the increased demand is not being met with the funding that is required.

We've already heard about the 5,000 learners across colleges in Wales who are studying without the associated funding to properly support them. In my own constituency, there are around 1,000 students currently in colleges without the funding in place to provide the support that they need. We've failed to fund that demand. We risk fewer places, fewer courses and less support for the young people that I talked about right at the opening of my contribution today, which are those young people who aren't in work, those young people who aren't currently in training and aren't able to see that future that we need them to be able to see.  The risk is a NEET crisis getting worse and not better.

But funding is only one part of the solution, and that's why our Welsh Conservative amendment is so important, and that's why we're calling on the Welsh Government to encourage that greater collaboration between those colleges and the private sector. Because we do have a bit of a strange situation in Wales at the moment, where many of us across the Chamber will be aware that employers are struggling to find people with the right skills while young people are struggling to find clear routes into work. So, something's not quite matching up. I'm sure that the Minister will speak about the skills audit that's under way, and I really hope that business is right at the heart of that thinking as well. Because employers can help those colleges understand the skills that industries need, colleges can give businesses access to the next generation of talent, and learners can gain the experience and understanding of the workplace that make the difference between finishing education and finding a career.

An example of this, Llywydd, is in the defence sector. We know that UK defence investment in Wales accounts for around about £1 billion a year into our Welsh industries. So, why wouldn't we want Welsh colleges to work with the defence sector to make sure our young people are equipped to take advantage of the opportunities that are there for them in the future? The same applies to construction, engineering, energy and many other sectors on which Wales's economy depends so importantly.

So, this isn't about telling young people what career they should choose, it's about giving them the opportunity, the experience and the choice to be able to move into a world of work. The Welsh Conservatives believe that every learner should be able to choose a path that works for them. That's why it's important that this motion and our amendment is supported. We need properly funded colleges, stronger links between education and industry and a Welsh Government focused on creating opportunities for our young people. Diolch yn fawr iawn.

contributions.text_english:
I'd like to thank Lynne Neagle for bringing this important debate to the Chamber today. Before the summer recess, I raised the situation at Coleg y Cymoedd, which has a campus in my constituency, in Nantgarw. Across its four campuses, there were hundreds of prospective learners placed on waiting lists due to funding constraints at that point. Many had applied for construction, manufacturing and other vocational courses, but even now, with the term under way, 400 learners have had to enrol on their second or third-choice courses, while 40 of them remain on waiting lists.

So, we are now just a year away from the roll-out of VCSEs, the vocational certificate of secondary education, for 14 to 16-year-olds. The situation at Coleg y Cymoedd clearly demonstrates there is already strong demand among young people for vocational education. So, with just one year to go until the roll-out, I wondered how the Welsh Government is planning to ensure the VCSEs are delivered consistently across all schools in Wales and, crucially, joined up with further education, apprenticeships and the skills needs that employers want.

I stand today in support of the motion, not because I agree with everything that Labour did in Government—and, to be clear, I don't—but because the facts in the motion today are true: too many young people in Wales are not in education, employment or training. Demand for college places is up, but the funding has not followed suit, and that is a crucial policy failure that must be addressed.

The motion today discusses a crisis amongst young people who are not in education, employment or training, alongside the lifelong scarring that follows. Now, we know that the statistics are dire. As Sam just shared with us, in the year ending December 2025, 17 per cent of 16 to 24-year-olds were not in education, employment or training. That's 56,800 young people who are unable to participate in the economy. Wales was the only UK nation where those statistics rose year on year, with a 5.5 per cent increase. That is a stark failure of the Government in this place to deliver for our young people. It's also a huge missed opportunity for our economy and for our public finances. If we could get just half of those young people into full-time employment, the Welsh Government would generate over £90 million in income tax receipts. And that's before you consider the wider benefits that come with a larger consumer base and a greater number of young people who are engaged in the economy.

Now, colleges are one of our main routes for young people to escape the NEET trap. The motion is right to recognise that the record levels of demand are imposing financial pressures on these organisations. Colleges across Wales are being forced to turn students away because they simply do not have the resources to place them on courses. I'm really pleased to be able to contribute to today's debate. I had the privilege of leading on higher education and further education in the last two years of the previous Welsh Labour Government. I'd just like to echo the point made by my colleague Lynne Neagle about how pleased we were to be able to allocate that additional £20 million to FE. But that need for additional funding is an upward trajectory, Deputy Minister, and this is a really clear message that you need to take from today's debate about that need for additional funding.

One thing I loved when I held that role was the ability to get out and about across Wales, meeting learners and the staff who support them. There were, and are, challenges, but the passion, the dedication to strive and achieve and deliver the very best learning outcomes was clear. That experience will shape my comments today, and I want to start by mentioning the new Welsh Government's higher education review. Now, this is important. The sector does face issues, and it's right that these are looked at, but the focus just on HE stands in direct contrast to the approach that we took in Government. That was based on ensuring the participation and sustainability of the whole tertiary system, and I am concerned that, without that focus, there's a very real danger that the focus on further education will be lost and its funding displaced also. I hope that this is something the Welsh Government will address when responding to the debate.

And what will the impact be if we lose this focus on FE? Well, we know that FE plays a key role in providing both vocational and academic pathways, particularly, as others have mentioned, for those young people most at risk of disengaging from education. Indeed, I would suggest that there is, in fact, a moral imperative for the Government to focus on FE to address this challenge.

On Monday, I visited Coleg y Cymoedd's Aberdare campus in my constituency, and my thanks to the staff and students who took the time to talk to me there as part of Adult Learners Week. There were some really excellent examples of mature learners re-engaging with education, meeting the need in the way that only FE can. This is another area where there is considerable demand, as I mentioned in my education question earlier today. This is a pattern that has been noted in several years. Those adult learners looking to re-engage should not have to lose out.

My conversations with staff and learners in Coleg y Cymoedd sketched out a very similar picture. Overall, that college, just one campus—. That college has over 5,500 full-time learners of all ages on its books, the majority aged 16 to 17, though. But, astonishingly, only just over 83 per cent are funded. Can I take a second just to reinforce that? Nearly one in five of the college's full-time students aren't funded. On the Aberdare campus, that's not just a stat, but 600 individual learners. Without funding, they are in real danger of disengaging.

So, there are 400 learners there at level 1 and level 2 who are not on their first-choice courses. That, in itself, represents a risk of disengagement. And for the first year ever, that particular campus has 40 learners that they haven't been able to place that are on a waiting list and unable to be enrolled, in real danger of disengaging from education forever. There were 80 learners there who they were only able to place on courses for two days a week. They would really like to be able to place them for much longer than that, and, of course, the less time they are placed in college, the more the risk of disengagement. That would need a hire drive for staff recruitment to accommodate, and, of course, that all comes down to funding.

There's been a 47 per cent increase in that campus alone in this year for individual development plans for learners with additional learning needs, and we all know that it needs resource to be able to cater for those needs. Now, I know a review of FE would not be a panacea, but it could shine a spotlight on the issues and help us work together to determine the solutions to put things right for our learners.

I want to close by reflecting on some of the benefits to the individual from engaging in FE: improved educational qualifications, a new path or journey, increased skills or enhanced employment opportunities. And crucially, as Public Health Wales reminds us, education is also one of the biggest preventative mechanisms for mental health as well. So, Deputy Minister, FE can change lives. Please remember that as you take forward your policy decisions over the coming Senedd term.

I'm glad also that we have the opportunity today to discuss NEETs, so I thank Lynne Neagle as well for bringing forward this really important debate, but also the chance to discuss why young people find themselves in this position as well. Not too long ago, I raised this issue here in the Senedd, particularly the long-term impact that being out of education, employment or training can have on a young person's chances in life. As one of the youngest Members in the Senedd—I think Ben actually might win the award just above me, just about—this is something that is really personal to me as well.

The recent Milburn report highlighted the real scale of this challenge, with around 56,000 young people in Wales. Again, that statistic's been bounced around, but that's 17 per cent of all 16 to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training. 

Now, there are lots of reasons why a young person might find themselves in this position. It could be difficulties at school, mental health, child poverty, transport, or simply not having the right support at the right time. In the constituency that I represent, Blaenau Gwent Caerffili Rhymni, we're seeing some of these challenges very clearly. Back in June, I raised this with the First Minister, pointing out that Blaenau Gwent has the highest proportion of residents aged 16 and over with no qualifications in Wales—that's 27.9 per cent—while Caerphilly is fourth among all local authorities.

Now, those figures are really concerning, but what concerns me more is what they can mean for a young person that's growing up in these communities. That's why early intervention really matters as well. We need to support young people before they reach the point of completely disengaging, and I've seen some really good examples of this in my own constituency. A couple of weeks ago, I visited ACT training in Ebbw Vale. They're supporting young people who, for all sorts of reasons, haven't found that typical conventional route from school into further education, training or employment. And I just want to put on the record as well my thanks to all of the staff there for the work that they do, because it was really inspiring, that visit. And there was one thing that really stood out to me that one of the staff said during that visit. They told me that, for some of the young people that they work with, the support that they provide can quite literally be the difference between life and death for that young person, and I think that really brings home again the real seriousness of this situation. Because we can talk about NEET rates and percentages like I did at the start, but, for that young person, this isn't a statistic. It's their life.

Further education and training have a huge role to play, but there are also wider barriers as well that can make it so hard for a young person to take that next step. If they're struggling with their mental health, they may not be in a position to engage. If they’re growing up in child poverty, like so many do in my constituency, they may not have the money for travel, equipment, or the stability that they need to take up an opportunity, if that opportunity's there. And particularly in the Valleys, transport, as we know, can be a real barrier. You can have a college course, apprenticeship or job available, but if a young person can't get there reliably or affordably that opportunity is, effectively, out of reach for them.

And that's why this has to be a cross-Government issue. Education and skills are a big part of the answer, and having those spaces as well is so important. But so are mental health, tackling child poverty, transport, the economy, and support for young people and their families.

Not every young person is going to follow the same path. Some will go to university, some into apprenticeships, some straight into employment, and some might take a little longer to find their route as well, and all of those options are okay. But what matters is that they have the opportunity to find it. A young person growing up in Blaenau Gwent Caerffili Rhymni should have the same chances to succeed as someone growing up anywhere else in Wales, because talent is spread equally across the whole of Wales, but opportunity isn't. Diolch.

I'll be speaking in favour of the motion. There are two issues at the heart of this motion: the number of young people not in education, employment or training, whom I shall refer to as NEETs, and whether our further education colleges have the capacity to meet current demand.

Starting with NEETs, the motion is right to refer to long-term scarring. A Scottish longitudinal study found that young people who are NEET at 16 to 19 were 2.8 times as likely to be unemployed or economically inactive 10 years later. At the societal level, with an ageing population, we need our young people to be productive as older generations leave the workforce. Also, we should develop the skills and potential of young people already living here, rather than relying on recruiting workers from overseas to support an ageing population.

Before moving on from NEETs, I want briefly to address AI. On GCSE results day this year, a young constituent e-mailed me because she was concerned about the impact of artificial intelligence on jobs. Young people are well aware of AI, and I would be misleading the Chamber if I said young people have nothing to worry about, because the Open University’s 2026 business barometer found that 19 per cent of employers surveyed had reduced early career recruitment, and, among those employers, 42 per cent attributed that reduction to the wider adoption of AI doing more entry-level tasks. Our young people are therefore now competing with both human and non-human intelligences for jobs. That makes the role of further education colleges in providing young people with skills and routes into productive work as important as ever.

Turning to FE colleges, I want to focus in the second part of my speech on Coleg y Cymoedd, which serves communities across my constituency of Blaenau Gwent Caerffili Rhymni, and I thank principal Jonathan Morgan for providing the following figures. Coleg y Cymoedd has provisionally enrolled 5,534 full-time learners this year, compared with 4,888 last year—an increase of more than 13 per cent in a single year. Yet it is funded for only around 4,596 learners, leaving a gap of more than 900 places, which the college estimates equates to a funding pressure of around £3 million. The consequences of supporting substantially more learners than are funded include increased class sizes and greater pressure on teaching staff, potentially compromising the quality of the learning experience.

On top of this, the number of learners with additional learning needs or individual development plans at Coleg y Cymoedd has risen from 309 to 454 in a single year—an increase of 47 per cent. It is absolutely to be welcomed that more young people with additional learning needs are accessing further education, but that increased participation requires additional funding. Without it, greater pressure is placed on specialist support teams, well-being provision and teaching staff. Yet funding has not kept pace—far from it. The Welsh FE sector received £21.5 million of increased participation funding in 2025-26. The equivalent allocation available in 2026-27 is £6.25 million. Coleg y Cymoedd's view is that restoring the previous level would provide an immediate means of addressing current demand pressures. These figures highlight the need to fund increased participation.

I agree with the case for increased participation funding set out in this motion, but funding must also come with scrutiny. As the Welsh Government considers future FE funding, it should look not only at how many places are required, but also at what those places are delivering. Are learners completing their courses? Are they gaining qualifications employers value? And are we training people in the skills Wales actually needs? Because further education should be a bridge into skilled work and genuine opportunity. For these reasons, while funding must come with rigorous scrutiny and proof of outcomes, I support the motion. More of our young people should have the opportunity to progress in life, both for their own sake and for the sake of society as a whole.

contributions.text_english:
We know there is a crisis of young people not being in education, employment or training, and the long-term scarring impact this has on their future health, earnings and life chances. If they're not in education between 16 and 18, the chance of them joining education after 18 or reaching employment reduces, and reduces rapidly.

As a former FE college lecturer and college governor, I welcome the increased participation of young people in further education colleges across Wales. It's very welcome, the rising demand for vocational and technical education. We need plumbers, we need hairdressers, we need electricians, we need decorators. We know we need those. In Britain, there were 981,000 young people aged 16 to 24 not in employment, education or training between April and June, according to the Office for National Statistics. But what shifts have happened there? We've got a lost generation of young people, and they're going to be lost forever unless urgent action is taken. And that really does fall on the Welsh Government to start taking some of this action.

What's happened over time has been the composition of this inactive group. The proportion who are inactive due to sickness or disability has more than doubled since 2005. I find it difficult to believe that almost a third of people who were NEETs in 2025 had health problems to such an extent that they were unable to engage in either education, training or employment. Other reasons are people having health and caring responsibilities and those who do not want or need employment. Those who do not want or need employment rose sharply during the same period, to reach 23 per cent of NEETs in 2025. I find it alarming that there will be some, the wealthy—probably sat on the benches opposite us—who actually have no need to work. But there's an awful lot of people who, if they're not in employment, are getting by on benefits.

At the same time, the share of young people inactive due to caring reasons has dropped, which is good news, but, again, the unpaid carers who we all meet fairly regularly keep on telling us about the problems. Those aged 16 and 17 who are likely to have been inactive for other reasons over the past few years, what happens then? They don't want to go to school. Lots of people don't want to carry on in school, school isn't for them, but that's not the end of education, that's not the end of training and that doesn't mean that they can never work. We have the Welsh Government's young person's guarantee scheme and that scheme is greatly welcomed.

Colleges and private training providers are the only option when direct movement into employment is not available. Private training providers, many of whom do an excellent job, lack capacity to train large numbers of young people. Evidence consistently shows that remaining in education post 16 is critical to young people's long-term life outcomes. It's also a point at which young people face a major decision of continuing in academic education or pursuing vocational education—a choice that can be difficult for those with limited guidance or family support. A lot of this comes down to what type of jobs you know, and most young people, what jobs do they know? They know teachers because they see them every day, they know what their families do, they know what their neighbours do, but there's a whole range of jobs that they know nothing about. A former Member of this Senedd who became a barrister did so because he went on training days with a barrister in Swansea. Now, that's something that is incredibly good, but we can't leave the future of young people to that sort of chance, can we?

Many young people want to go to college, and I recognise the financial pressures on colleges, if only because they keep on telling me. But no 16 to 18-year-old should be unable to attend a college because not enough places are funded. For colleges that provide training that is not funded by the Welsh Government, the amount is limited by financial pressure. There is a need for the Welsh Government to fund all the places that are needed. If we don't want NEETs, let's not be the people who create the NEETs by not providing training places for young people. And if young people who cannot get a job or get on a college course become NEET, it's not their fault, it's ours, or should I say, the Welsh Government's. The Government needs to fund further education colleges so that everyone who wants to go to college can go. This is why I support this motion today. It's important that every young person gets the opportunity they deserve.

I find it difficult to believe that almost a third of people who were NEETs in 2025 had health problems to such an extent that they were unable to engage in either education, training or employment. Other reasons are people having health and caring responsibilities and those who do not want or need employment. Those who do not want or need employment rose sharply during the same period, to reach 23 per cent of NEETs in 2025. I find it alarming that there will be some, the wealthy—probably sat on the benches opposite us—who actually have no need to work. But there's an awful lot of people who, if they're not in employment, are getting by on benefits.

At the same time, the share of young people inactive due to caring reasons has dropped, which is good news, but, again, the unpaid carers who we all meet fairly regularly keep on telling us about the problems. Those aged 16 and 17 who are likely to have been inactive for other reasons over the past few years, what happens then? They don't want to go to school. Lots of people don't want to carry on in school, school isn't for them, but that's not the end of education, that's not the end of training and that doesn't mean that they can never work. We have the Welsh Government's young person's guarantee scheme and that scheme is greatly welcomed.

Colleges and private training providers are the only option when direct movement into employment is not available. Private training providers, many of whom do an excellent job, lack capacity to train large numbers of young people. Evidence consistently shows that remaining in education post 16 is critical to young people's long-term life outcomes. It's also a point at which young people face a major decision of continuing in academic education or pursuing vocational education—a choice that can be difficult for those with limited guidance or family support. A lot of this comes down to what type of jobs you know, and most young people, what jobs do they know? They know teachers because they see them every day, they know what their families do, they know what their neighbours do, but there's a whole range of jobs that they know nothing about. A former Member of this Senedd who became a barrister did so because he went on training days with a barrister in Swansea. Now, that's something that is incredibly good, but we can't leave the future of young people to that sort of chance, can we?

Many young people want to go to college, and I recognise the financial pressures on colleges, if only because they keep on telling me. But no 16 to 18-year-old should be unable to attend a college because not enough places are funded. For colleges that provide training that is not funded by the Welsh Government, the amount is limited by financial pressure. There is a need for the Welsh Government to fund all the places that are needed. If we don't want NEETs, let's not be the people who create the NEETs by not providing training places for young people. And if young people who cannot get a job or get on a college course become NEET, it's not their fault, it's ours, or should I say, the Welsh Government's. The Government needs to fund further education colleges so that everyone who wants to go to college can go. This is why I support this motion today. It's important that every young person gets the opportunity they deserve.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you for bringing this motion to the Chamber, and can I thank everyone for their powerful contributions to this debate? I find myself agreeing with all the points that have been made. You will not find a greater champion for skills, tertiary education and the futures of young people than me, and I'm glad that we have had this opportunity to highlight the importance of supporting our young people, moving forward. I'm sure we all want to see increased opportunities for young people, a stronger skills system, a stronger and more flourishing economy, and young people supported by a committed and able workforce.

The NEETs statistics that have been highlighted by so many of you are completely unacceptable for us in Wales. The fact that 50,000 plus young people are NEETs between 16 and 24 is not where we want to be as a nation, with about 17 per cent of young people facing reduced life chances at a very early age. We can do better than this. We must do better than this.

This is a situation this Welsh Government has inherited in many ways. As I set out in my statement on priorities for skills and tertiary education earlier this Senedd term, supporting young people into learning and work is a key priority for this Government. We want a system that develops skills, builds confidence and creates genuine pathways into employment and further learning. Our ambition is one education system and skills system for Wales, a system that's accessible, coherent and of the highest quality, and one that supports people throughout their lives and contributes to economic prosperity and social cohesion.

Now, earlier this year—again, it's been mentioned many times—Alan Milburn published his interim report into young people and work. His report highlights that, across the UK, one in eight young people are NEETs. We can't underestimate the impact that this has on young people and their families and the lasting effects on future earnings, health, well-being and life chances. So too must we consider the impact on communities and the local economy, and the sense of belonging and a social and economic infrastructure that allows them opportunities to flourish. 

What the Alan Milburn report also highlights is that about 70 per cent of those young people that are NEETs are economically inactive. That is, they are not actively looking for work. That clearly shows that there are underlying issues as well around that 70 per cent to do with mental health, to do with disability, to do with ALN, to do with childcare. There are so many other barriers that we need to recognise. These are the young people furthest away from the labour market. So, in terms of that 70 per cent, what we need to do is have an integrated holistic strategy for tackling NEETs.

NEETs aren't the responsibility solely of education and skills. It has to involve health, it has to involve social services, it has to involve transport, training and housing, and all those issues that many of you have raised today. So, I am committing to develop a holistic NEETs strategy for Wales—[Interruption.] Yes, go on.

contributions.text_english: What we do know is that many of those NEETs are NEETs because they can't get on to an education course in a college. Will you fund all the courses for all those young people who want to go on and stop them being NEETs and get them into education?
contributions.text_original: What we do know is that many of those NEETs are NEETs because they can't get on to an education course in a college. Will you fund all the courses for all those young people who want to go on and stop them being NEETs and get them into education?

contributions.text_english:
Thank you, Mike. I'm just coming on to that.

We need highly skilled people, we need to get people off that NEET register. I recognise the increased participation in further education. I've had numerous conversations with Medr and ColegauCymru, and I've had correspondence from individual colleges as well, as I'm sure everyone in this Senedd has. I recognise the challenges and I am monitoring the situation. We will know better by November what the exact data is. Although we are in very difficult and challenging financial circumstances at the moment—that is well known to everyone in this Chamber—I will be making a case for us to support the increased enrolments that we are seeing in FE colleges, because failing to do so would be to let down a whole group of young people who are the most vulnerable in our society. 

But my point is this: it is not only for colleges to support young people. As I mentioned, we need a wider approach, especially around that 70 per cent who have various difficulties in becoming active in looking for employment. We need to reduce the number of learners not in education, training and employment, but we need to involve other key partners as well, like apprenticeship providers and so on. We need to work closely with the business sector to ensure that employers are giving opportunities to young people to have a softer approach to work experience, and then maybe apprenticeships as well.

We see the increased enrolments as well around level 1 and level 2 courses, which are basic numeracy and literacy courses, which is why it is important that the Minister for education launched her numeracy and literacy plan last week, so that we put the basics in place in our schools to avoid those young people having difficulties later on in life. That is why I fully support the development of the VCSEs that are coming on board in our schools in 2027. They will give opportunities at a very early age for young people to make choices around vocational studies, more academic pathways, or a hybrid of both. I think that that is a way forward as well to ensure that our young people develop the skills, talent and interests that they have in as wide a set of options as possible.

I find myself in full agreement with all of the points that have been made about the importance of skills and supporting young people into education, training and employment. I am monitoring the situation in terms of how we can support that financially and we will be making a statement around this in due course. I will finish off, Llywydd—I know my time is up.

I'm told that I've got seven minutes and 45 seconds, so that's very precise. Can I thank everybody who contributed to the debate? It was great to see so many speakers from across the Chamber, and I'll try to respond to some of the points that were made. 

Thank you, Sam, for your contribution. I think you started the trend of highlighting some really stark figures in terms of young people who are NEET, and also the numbers of students that there are unfunded places for. That's been a common theme across the debate. Thank you for sharing with us your visit to Coleg Cambria, and it's great to hear that Members are visiting their local colleges. I'm told that there is already a great deal of collaboration between colleges and the private sector, and you highlighted how important it is to match the skills that learners are studying with the employment opportunities that are available in their local communities.

contributions.text_english:
Can I thank Zaynub Akbar for her contributions and her advocacy on behalf of Coleg y Cymoedd? Zaynub also identified some of the really stark figures that there are in terms of young people on waiting lists. For me, the reason I'm passionate about this issue is not just because we want young people to have the skills to get into employment. It's because being NEET is a serious risk to young people's mental health, and it's absolutely critical that we hold on to those young people. And my fear is that those young people who are sitting on waiting lists will be lost to the system and we won't get them back.

Benjamin Hodge Mckenna, thank you for your contribution as well, and again for emphasising the stark figures that exist around young people not in education, training and employment. It is absolutely not good enough.

Can I thank my colleague Vikki Howells, who I know is particularly passionate about supporting the FE sector? Vikki highlighted the fact that these figures are on an upward trajectory. So they are something that has to be got to grips with. Because the figures, as a success story, are going in the right way, but unless we meet those pressures, that is going to rapidly turn into a problem.

Vikki, you highlighted as well the passion and the dedication that is seen in our colleges, and that's something that I've seen as well, the palpable commitment to supporting learners, and especially young people. I know that you're aware that I share your concerns about the higher education review. That's not to say that we don't think there's a need to look at the higher education sector, but my preference would have been to do it in a holistic way, in a joined-up way, looking at participation in post-16 more generally.

Vikki also, again—there are some great advocates for Coleg y Cymoedd here today—highlighted the issues in Coleg y Cymoedd, but also, importantly, mentioned the issues around ALN, and that is something that colleges are struggling with. I think, probably, there is some unmet need coming through from schools that colleges are grappling with. That's why it's vital that, when we look at funding ALN, we are also thinking about the colleges.

Thank you, Niamh, for your very passionate contribution about the importance of preventing young people becoming NEET. This is about a complex range of problems, as you highlighted. It was good to hear that you'd visited ACT Training. I've got an ACT centre in my constituency. One of the things you said that particularly resonated with me was that this can be a matter of life and death, and I have heard that too. These are some of the most vulnerable learners, and that is why it is so critical that we hold on to them. I also very much agree with you that talent is spread evenly, but opportunity isn't, and that's the challenge for us to tackle.

Thank you, Joshua Kim, as well, for your contribution and, again, your advocacy for Coleg y Cymoedd, and for raising the issues around AI, which I think are far too big for me to address in a debate of this nature, but undoubtedly are very relevant to the challenges that young people and providers are grappling with at the moment.

Thank you, Mike, for your contribution, which I know comes from your background as a former FE lecturer, and for highlighting some of the differences in reasons why young people are becoming NEET. I think some of the figures that you've highlighted about economic inactivity show the complexity of the reasons why young people aren't in education and employment.

Thank you, Jane, for your contribution. I know how important the college is to you, and you've spoken up for the college before. As you've highlighted, it's particularly important in rural Wales that we hold on to those young people in the communities and that they're able to stay in their communities and build a future. That's vitally important.

Can I thank Cefin Campbell for his contribution? I know, Cefin, that this is something that you are passionate about, and obviously we've discussed it many times on different sides of this Chamber. It's good to hear your commitment to addressing these issues. I would flag to you as well that we've got things like the youth engagement and progression framework, which is a really positive, holistic framework, and I hope that the Government will continue to be committed to that. We've heard in the debate as well about the importance of work experience. I know careers sits with you now; that's vital as well and can prevent young people becoming NEET. And just as the public health Minister sits down beside you, that is, of course, a public health intervention.

It was good to hear that we're going to have more news on this. I recognise what you've said about November and that being a cut-off for when you will have the exact figures, but what I would say to you is that all this commitment that there's been to FE participation will have to be matched by action. I hope that when we get to that point in November, your advocacy for more funding for the sector—. It's been good that the Cabinet Minister for Finance has been in the Chamber for this debate and heard the commitment to FE. I think we all want to see that matched with action and more investment. Diolch yn fawr.

contributions.text_english: We'll move now to item 7, the Reform UK debate, Wales and the United Kingdom. I call on Adrian Mason to move the motion.
contributions.text_original: Symudwn at eitem 7, dadl Reform UK, Cymru a'r Deyrnas Unedig. Galwaf ar Adrian Mason i wneud y cynnig.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch. This motion before us concerns one of the most fundamental questions we can debate in this Chamber: the constitutional future of Wales and its place within the United Kingdom. Plaid Cymru's amendment says that Wales's constitutional future should be determined by the people of Wales. Well, of course, we're democrats, and the views of the people of Wales are fundamental. Too often now, debates about the union begin with what the alleged faults are, but we should also examine what the union means in practical terms for the people we represent.

Wales, today—we're here—has its own parliament, its own government, and substantial responsibility for its own domestic affairs. At the same time, we remain part of a wider United Kingdom, in which matters including defence, foreign affairs, monetary policy and most social security and state pensions are shared at UK level. That combination of devolved government and common UK institutions is built into the present constitutional settlement. It means we can be Welsh without having to choose between being Welsh and being British.

Diolch. This motion before us concerns one of the most fundamental questions we can debate in this Chamber: the constitutional future of Wales and its place within the United Kingdom. Plaid Cymru's amendment says that Wales's constitutional future should be determined by the people of Wales. Well, of course, we're democrats, and the views of the people of Wales are fundamental. Too often now, debates about the union begin with what the alleged faults are, but we should also examine what the union means in practical terms for the people we represent.

Wales, today—we're here—has its own parliament, its own government, and substantial responsibility for its own domestic affairs. At the same time, we remain part of a wider United Kingdom, in which matters including defence, foreign affairs, monetary policy and most social security and state pensions are shared at UK level. That combination of devolved government and common UK institutions is built into the present constitutional settlement. It means we can be Welsh without having to choose between being Welsh and being British.

Our national identity does not depend upon constitutional separation. And the union is not simply a constitutional concept. It operates every day. People live in Wales and work in England. Businesses in Wales trade naturally with businesses in England. Families live on both sides of the border. Students, patients, trains, roads, supply chains—they all cross the border.

For much of north-east Wales in particular, the border is not an edge of an economy, it runs right through the middle of it. That economic integration can be seen in the Welsh Government's own figures. Its latest trade survey estimates that businesses in Wales sold about £48.2 million-worth of goods and services to the rest of the United Kingdom, and international sales were about £24.2 billion. So, Welsh businesses sold about twice as much to the rest of the United Kingdom as they did to the whole international market combined, and that's the Welsh Government's figures.

contributions.text_english:
So, that is not an argument that Wales could not trade with England if it became independent, clearly it could, but it does demonstrate the sheer scale of the economic relationship that already exists in the United Kingdom. And that relationship operates with a common currency, a common monetary system and no exchange rate between Wales and England. We use sterling. Monetary policy is set through the Bank of England of the United Kingdom as a whole. A business, say, in Tenby buying goods from Birmingham does not have to think about currency conversions. A worker living in Powys and earning a salary across the border doesn't have to think about exchange rates. A pension does not change currency when somebody moves from Colwyn Bay to Chester. These things are easily taken for granted precisely because they happen every day.

There's also a pooling of resources. We hear often in this Chamber about fair funding, and there are legitimate arguments about the Barnett formula, individual spending decisions and how resources should be distributed, but that debate should also include the whole picture. The latest Office for National Statistics's country and regional public finance figures show that the public expenditure attributed to Wales substantially exceeds public revenues attributed to Wales. And the gap is phenomenal: in 2024-25 it was approximately £23 billion. Now, we should be precise about what this actually means. It's a measure of Wales within the present United Kingdom fiscal system, it's not automatically a prediction of the budget deficit of an independent Wales, but it should not be simply ignored.

One of the features of the United Kingdom is that revenue and expenditure are pooled across different parts of the country. At times, alternative areas contribute distinct amounts and have different spending needs. That pooling of resources is part of what a fiscal union actually means. The same principle can be seen in state pensions and much of social security. These remain UK-wide responsibilities under the current settlement. State pensions, pension credit, universal credit and disability benefit are all matters that basically are still reserved to the United Kingdom. Defence is shared. Foreign affairs are shared. Monetary policy is shared. There are therefore practical institutions behind the word 'union'. And none of this prevents Wales from having its own democratic institutions. The Senedd legislates in devolved areas, Welsh Ministers make decisions in those areas. The argument is not, therefore, a choice between having a Welsh voice and not having a Welsh voice. The present constitutional model combines Welsh self-government in devolved matters with participation in wider UK institutions.

Now, look, none of this means that the present system is perfect. No constitutional settlement is ever perfect. There will always be arguments about where power should lie, how money should be allocated and whether a particular decision should be taken in Cardiff or Westminster. We see it all the time. These are legitimate debates. But changing a constitutional settlement is entirely a different proposition. Plaid Cymru is clear about its ultimate aim. Its constitution states that it seeks independence for Wales in Europe. If independence is put forward as an alternative, it is reasonable to ask what would replace the arrangements I have just described. What currency would Wales use? Would it continue using sterling? If so, what influence would an independent Welsh Government have over monetary policy? Would a new Welsh currency eventually be created? What would happen to the fiscal arrangements that presently operate across the United Kingdom? How would pensions and social security liability be divided? What proportion of the UK assets and, crucially, liabilities would be negotiated? And what trading arrangements would apply if the independent Wales sought membership of the European Union while England remained outside it?

These are not reasons to avoid a constitutional debate, they are the substance of a constitutional debate. This is why I think we need to move beyond slogans on all sides. Those who advocate for constitutional change should explain what that change means in practical terms, and those who defend existing arrangements should be prepared to explain how they can work better. The people of Wales should be given the facts as opposed to simply competing assertions. For me, there are some straightforward questions that should apply whenever major constitutional change is proposed. What issue are we seeking to solve? What evidence is there that changing the constitution will solve it? What are the financial consequences? What happens to cross-border services? How will the new arrangements work, and who will be accountable for delivering them? These are sensible tests when a proposal concerns further devolution, independence or any other fundamental constitutional change.

And there is one final point: this debate should never become a test of somebody's Welshness. There are people deeply proud to be Welsh who support independence. There are people equally proud to be Welsh who support the union. Constitutional preference does not determine national identity.

So, Llywydd, as we consider this motion, and the amendments, I hope we can look beyond labels. We should examine the issues we already share: the economic relationship that already exists, the pooling of resources, the common currency, and the shared system of pension, social security, defence and international representation. Apologies for going over. Because whenever Wales ultimately chooses, decisions of this magnitude deserve to be made on the basis of evidence, practical detail and a clear understanding of the consequences. That is what I believe is the absolute basis for which this constitutional debate should take place. Thank you.

contributions.text_english: I now call on the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution to formally move amendment 1, tabled in the name of Heledd Fychan.

contributions.text_english: Thank you very much. I now call on Huw Thomas to move amendment 2, tabled in the name of Lynne Neagle.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Lywydd. In a debate that too often doesn't allow for nuance, I'm going to try to insert some. Welsh Labour believes that Wales's future is more secure and more prosperous as part of the United Kingdom. Secondly, we also believe that sovereignty ultimately rests within the people of Wales. The union doesn't have a God-given right to exist. It has to demonstrate that it works for each part of the UK. And to that end, we agree and support the Plaid Cymru amendment that the constitution of Wales is a matter for the people of Wales. And as you've seen in our own amendment, we further believe that devolution is the settled will of the people of Wales. This has been tested at two referenda. A majority of Welsh MPs represent parties who support devolution. Even at the historic Senedd election in May and subsequent opinion polls, it is clear that, for a majority of Welsh people, their preferred constitutional settlement is devolution. And they want this place to work for them.

Now, as a Welsh-speaking Welshman born in west Wales, I'm occasionally asked why I'm not a member of Plaid Cymru. I know, imagine. [Laughter.] Putting aside that, for me, my Welsh identity is not in competition with my British one or indeed my European one. People can feel both or all three at the same time and not be any less Welsh or any less British. But putting that aside, the answer partly lies in a little phrase that I've carried around in my wallet for the last 20 years. It's on my Labour Party membership card. It declares that

'by the strength of our common endeavour we achieve more than we achieve alone'.

contributions.text_english: In other words, strength comes with unity; together we are stronger. That is the ethos that allowed Robert Owen, a Welshman from Newtown, to establish the pioneering co-operative community in New Lanark, Scotland, and then to expand that co-operative movement across Britain in the nineteenth century. When Aneurin Bevan established the health service, he didn't just do that in Tredegar or just in Wales, but he did that across the United Kingdom. And today, even within a devolved settlement, people from all parts of this country continue to benefit from sharing resources and expertise across the political borders of the United Kingdom.
contributions.text_original: Mewn geiriau eraill, mewn undod mae nerth; gyda'n gilydd yn gryfach. Dyna'r ethos ganiataodd i Gymro o'r Drenewydd, Robert Owen, sefydlu'r gymuned gydweithredol arloesol yn New Lanark yn yr Alban, ac yna ehangu'r symudiad cydweithredol hwnnw ledled Prydain yn y bedwaredd ganrif ar bymtheg. Pan sefydlodd Aneurin Bevan y gwasanaeth iechyd, wnaeth e ddim gwneud hynny jest yn Nhredegar neu jest yng Nghymru, ond ledled y Deyrnas Gyfunol. A hyd heddiw, hyd yn oed o fewn setliad datganoledig, mae pobl o bob cwr o'r wlad yn parhau i fanteisio o rannu adnoddau ac arbenigedd ar draws ffiniau gwleidyddol y Deyrnas Gyfunol.

contributions.text_english:
When Welsh miners went on strike for their livelihoods and their industry, they didn't do so in isolation, they did so in concert with workers in England and Scotland, and received support from communities across the UK, including, famously, the gay community in London. We've heard today about the nuclear industry: a project in south-west England underpinned by a supply chain in south Wales, and a project in north Wales unlocked by engineering excellence of a British firm growing out of the north-west of England. And as for those high-growth Welsh companies that the economy Minister referenced earlier, when they want to raise capital for growth, they can do so easily with seamless access to the best place to do so on the planet, in the City of London.

Now, I, too, do not pretend that the union, as it stands, is perfect. It is too centralised, it is too unequal, and there is a clear case for reform—lower case. [Laughter.] There are some in this Chamber, no doubt, who will say that the levels of poverty in Wales would justify independence, but if you park the fact that independence would cost every person in Wales £7,000 and result in catastrophic cuts to public services, or if you don't acknowledge that, since 1999, the devolved nations and regions, including Wales, have actually outperformed the rest of the country. If you ignore all of that, I would bet that those who want independence because Wales is poorer than other parts of the UK would still want independence if Wales was richer than other parts of the UK. Such is the dogmaticalness of their position.

On these benches, we believe in the redistribution of wealth, using the resources of richer areas to lift outcomes across the country. And we also believe in decisions being taken at the right level of Government. That's why we want to see more decisions being taken by local councils—power devolved not just to Wales, but out of Cardiff Bay. There are, then, of course, decisions that are best taken within Wales. I would argue, despite the myriad challenges posed by Tory austerity in the period from 2010, that period nevertheless shows devolution working, with the Welsh Government able to protect Wales and Welsh institutions in a way that wasn't possible during the 1980s, and now—

contributions.text_english:
I welcome this discussion. I was brought up on a council estate in Wrexham and I still live there, and I know there aren't many people from that background in this Chamber, so I'm always conscious of the enormous privilege that it is to stand here and represent the community that raised me. I was also a county councillor for almost 20 years, so I also understand people's frustrations as well. Over the decades, I've watched communities like mine lose industries, lose opportunities and lose public services, all whilst the cost of living has skyrocketed.

So, I can understand why, after years of that, people start to wonder whether managed decline is just our fate, but I don't believe that it is, because I come from a country that has endured. Over the centuries, through enormous upheaval, despite everything that's happened to us, Cymru is still here. Our language is a living language, our culture is thriving and our communities still carry a powerful sense of identity and belonging. And we still have that stubborn determination to be Welsh.

Now, we've got quite the inheritance, but our responsibility isn't simply to preserve it, it's to decide what we're going to do with it. And that, I think, exposes one of the fundamental differences between Reform's politics and ours. Last week, we heard a Reform Member tell this chamber that the British empire was, ultimately, a force for good in the world. Now, many people in Cymru and across the world would profoundly disagree with that view, but it tells us something about the political imagination on offer, doesn't it? Because theirs looks backwards to an idea of what they believe Britain once was. Ours looks forward to what Cymru can become.

Now, I didn't come into politics to recreate some rose-tinted version of the last century. I want to build the next one, to build a country with the power, confidence and the ambition to improve people's lives. And that, for me, is exactly what this constitutional journey is about. It’s about confidence: the confidence to believe that more than 3 million people are perfectly capable of shaping our own future, the confidence to stop asking whether we're too small, too poor or too dependent and to start asking what we can create—a country that takes responsibility for our future, that co-operates confidently with others in these islands and right across the world, and that refuses to accept that decline is the best we can hope for. My community deserves better than that. Communities across Wales deserve better than that. Because history should give us more than nostalgia. It should give us confidence—confidence that the next chapter of our national story won't be written by someone else, somewhere else; it will be written by us.

The people of Wales have elected the first-ever Plaid Cymru Government, the first Welsh Government in over 600 years answerable solely to the people of Wales. And that matters, because, for too long, too many decisions about our country have been made elsewhere. But the future of Wales belongs here, and it's for the people of Wales to decide what comes next.
