contributions.text_english:
Addressing the motion before us, let me remind Members what the First Minister promised before the election. It was to establish a national commission on Wales's constitutional feature, not push for independence after 100 days. Yet after meeting the leaders of Sinn Féin and the SNP, this administration now appears to be charging full pelt towards independence. The joint Plaid, Sinn Féin and SNP agreement declares, and I quote,

‘Momentum is behind our movements; we believe that constitutional change is coming.’

The people of Wales deserve to know exactly what that means, exactly what it will cost, and exactly who will pay. Only last year, the First Minister declared that there was business to do right now. That meant, he stated, improvements in health, education, families, jobs, the environment and farming. And on that point, I agree. There is business to do, urgent business, serious business, and yet, instead of getting on with that, we seem to be heading down a constitutional rabbit hole.

Welsh families are worried about the Welsh NHS. They're worried about the cost of living. They're worried about whether their children will find jobs and build a future. And what is the answer from Plaid Cymru? More division, more distraction, more constitutional theatre.

After 100 days, this administration should be focused on what matters to the people of Wales. Patients are still waiting too long for treatment. Front-line services remain under pressure, and unemployment is too high. Energy bills for households and business are disastrous. Breaking the union will not fix any of this; it will make it worse.

And then there is the cost. Wales simply cannot afford the independence experiment. The Office for National Statistics demonstrated that the net fiscal deficit for Wales in 2024-25 was between £22 billion and £23 billion. And your own Minister, Dafydd Trystan Davies, Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution stated, and I quote,

‘it is plainly evident that Wales is a net fiscal beneficiary of the United Kingdom.’

What would be needed to pay for this? The answer: higher taxes and more borrowing. This is not a plan. It is a slow-motion fiscal car crash dressed up as a national project. And who pays? Who picks up the bill? The answer is simple: the Welsh taxpayer, Welsh families.

Leaving the United Kingdom would mean walking away from the benefits of a larger union, shared resources, fiscal transfers and economic scale. It's a gamble with people's jobs, mortgages, pensions—a gamble doomed to failure.

Then there is the plan to devolve the Crown Estate. This isn't the magic bullet Plaid claim. There is no Scottish-style windfall and no pot of gold at the end of the rainbow. I'm a proud Conservative and I'm a proud unionist, because the United Kingdom is more than a political arrangement; we are a shared family of nations, which for centuries have had people in Wales living and working alongside and trading with other parts of the United Kingdom. We built industries together, we went through the industrial revolution together, we fought tyranny together, we created wealth, improved living standards and built communities together, and our history is Welsh and British. And those identities are not in conflict with one another; they strengthen who and what we are. The union means that someone born in Wales can study, work, establish a business, raise a family and retire anywhere they want in the whole of the United Kingdom. And, most importantly, it means that when adversity strikes, whether that's war, economic crisis, natural disaster, pandemics, or even attempted AI takeovers of the planet, the strength and resources of the whole of the United Kingdom stand behind every single citizen across Britain.

As part of the UK, Wales is one of the world's six largest economies. We're protected by one of its finest armed forces. Llywydd, when people across Wales have been crying out for an NHS that works, for better education standards for our children, and for greater prosperity in our country, that's what this Government should be focused on. Prior to the election, that is what our First Minister—who can't even be bothered to turn up to this debate, by the way—promised the people of Wales. [Interruption.] Yes, I know it's embarrassing that he's missing. He's got his human shield here, Dafydd Trystan, to represent him, but he is missing from the debate, which I think is an important thing to note. The First Minister has very different priorities, because, instead of rolling his sleeves up and getting on with that day job, delivering on those issues, the First Minister's very first act after the summer recess and his holidays was to cosy up to Sinn Féin and the SNP to issue bold predictions, like Mystic Meg staring into the crystal ball, saying that Westminster is coming to an end and that Andy Burnham's going to be the last British Prime Minister. And then, of course, he signed a pact deliberately attempting to promote the break-up of the United Kingdom. That was his priority and it is shameful. But, in spite of the grandstanding, the First Minister, Plaid Cymru, and all those who support the break-up of the United Kingdom cannot even answer the most basic of questions about what would happen if Wales was ripped from the rest of the UK. What currency would an independent Wales use? There's no answer. Would it be the pound—would it be the currency of the UK they just left, or would it be a new Welsh currency that was practically worthless, or the euro? Would Welsh citizens—? I'll happily take an intervention.

contributions.text_english: Since the United Kingdom was formed, 65 countries have become independent. How many of those have asked to come back? And what is unique about Wales that you think Wales is incapable of running its own affairs?

contributions.text_english:
Let's get back to the questions, which you didn't answer, by the way, okay. So, what currency would we use? No answer. Would Welsh citizens retain the right, the automatic right that they currently have today, to live, work and study elsewhere in the UK? They can't tell us. Would Welsh businesses retain unfettered access to our most important market in England, Scotland and Northern Ireland? They have absolutely no idea. Would the so-called party of Wales seek to rejoin the European Union that was rejected—[Interruption.]—that was rejected by the people of Wales? And I know—[Interruption.] And I know it's an inconvenient truth for you to hear, but the people of Wales voted to leave the EU. Who would be our head of state? Who would be our head of state? They have no answer whatsoever. I know they want to abolish the monarchy, but who's going to be the president? No answer. Would taxes rise, spending fall, or borrowing go through the roof because you can't afford to pay for the unaffordable promises that you have made to the people of Wales because of that huge fiscal gap that would cost every single taxpayer, by the way, in the whole of our country, about £14,000 each and every single year? That's the reality. Would Wales have its own armed forces? Would you join NATO? Would you join NATO?

You cannot answer these things. And they're not technicalities; these concern people's jobs, savings, mortgages, pensions, national security and our clout on the international stage. I'm not prepared to take that risk. I firmly believe that Wales is better off in the United Kingdom and that the United Kingdom is better off with Wales right at the very centre of everything that it does. I'm proud to be a member of the Welsh Conservatives and the Conservative and Unionist Party.

Thank you, Llywydd. It's clear, in looking at the motion and the amendments tabled this afternoon, that there are two very different views on the future of Wales in this Chamber.

I will turn first of all to Reform's original motion. I'm sure that the irony will be palpable to all, as a party that makes great play of the importance of freedom of opinion seeks to limit the right of the people of Wales to have a constructive discussion on the future of our nation. A discussion on their own terms, that's all Reform are interested in. As the growth in support for constitutional change continues, their strategy of protecting the status quo of the UK and casting doubt on the benefits of devolution is contrary to the view of the majority of the people of Wales.

And let's turn now to the Labour amendment. Yes, warm words about devolution and all its benefits on paper, but as we saw over the two years of their partnership in power at both ends of the M4, they mean nothing in practice. Although the direction has come now to be more supportive of devolution from their new head in Downing Street, they are finding it difficult to even convince their own Members in Westminster of the need for further devolution.

In the election, the people of Wales made it clear that they wanted more powers over their own future, but they also made it perfectly clear that they don't believe that Labour is serious about acting on those aspirations, which brings me to the Plaid Cymru amendment. Simply, we believe that the people of Wales and the people of Wales alone should have the right to determine their own future. Those aren't constitutional dreams, but a fundamental right that is afforded to almost every other democratic nation across the world. In tabling our amendment today, we are seeking to unlock the conversation about the future of our nation. The other parties are determined to keep it under lock and key. Is this the best things can be for Wales?

During the summer, I went over to Slovenia, a nation with a million fewer people than Wales, a nation that insisted on its independence despite a challenging economic and social environment. But now it's a nation that has caused its economy to grow more than sevenfold over recent years, a nation that has benefited from its membership of the European Union, and a nation that has built its economy on the energy and tourism sectors. The comparison with Wales in that regard is quite clear.

Personally, I don't believe that Westminster is working for our nation, but the people of Wales should have the power to have their say on that issue, not Whitehall. To conclude, Llywydd, Matthew Rhys said last week,

The United Kingdom is the greatest nation in the history of the world. We gave parliamentary democracy, common law and the industrial age—I'm glad you're laughing, it's not funny. We defeated Napoleon. We abolished the slave trade—sorry to disappoint you. We stood against Hitler in 1940 when the rest of Europe had fallen.

And at every one of those moments, Wales was there. Wales has been at the centre of British history for generations. In 1485, Henry Tudor, a Welshman born in Pembroke castle, landed near Milford Haven. He marched through Wales, gathering men to his banner, the Red Dragon, and he took the crown at Bosworth. His granddaughter Queen Elizabeth I began the British empire, which was such a force for good in the world. Sorry, Carrie. Welsh minds then went on to shape the modern world. William Grove from Swansea invented the fuel cell in 1842, a technology the world is still using today.

In Mumbles, a constituency I used to represent as a councillor, we pioneered the world's first passenger railway. Merthyr became the largest ironworks on earth. In Swansea, we smelted so much of the world's copper that we were famously called Copperopolis, for your information. Welsh steam coal fuelled the Royal Navy, and the first cheque for £1 million was signed at the Coal Exchange in Cardiff—[Interruption.] Welsh iron made the—no, we haven't got enough time, thank you, and this is important—railway of the empire. Welsh coal powered the fleet that protected them.

When Britain went to war, Wales answered. At Rorke's Drift, in 1879, Wales's 24 Regiment of Foot held off thousands and won 11 Victoria Crosses in a single action. A Welsh Prime Minister, David Lloyd George, led us to victory in the great war. The Welsh Guards were formed in 1915 and have served this country in every major conflict since. In February 1941, Swansea endured three nights of the Blitz and our town did not break. In 1982, Welsh Guards gave their lives in the Falklands war, defending British people and British soil. That is our history.

Welsh blood, Welsh industry and Welsh genius are written into every chapter of the British story. So, when I look at the politics of Wales today, I see people in positions of power who are working to tear that story apart. Plaid claimed during the election that independence wouldn't be an issue, but now the mask has slipped. Their true colours have now been shown, thanks to their meeting with Sinn Féin, the political wing of the IRA. There are Members in this Chamber who want to break up the United Kingdom. They want to walk away from the shared resources that fund our schools, our hospitals, our pensions and our armed forces. They want to take Wales out of the most successful union the world has ever seen, and they can't even tell the people of Wales the basics of what currency we'd use or how we would pay our way.

For nearly 30 years of devolution, Cardiff Bay has been obsessed with the constitution—more politicians, more powers, more bureaucracy and more red tape. And through all of it, Wales has remained at the bottom of the UK for income, employment and for our health and education outcomes. Westminster Governments of every colour carry their share of blame. They have spent years apologising for Britain instead of celebrating us. They have allowed our history to be rewritten as a list of crimes. They have forced mass immigration and its terrible consequences on our people. They have let energy prices in the land of coal and steam rise to some of the highest in the developed world, and they have watched Welsh steel furnaces go cold. The people of Wales and the United Kingdom deserve better than a political class that is embarrassed by their own country. They want to abandon the values that made us great in the first place.

This month, September, marks my eighteenth anniversary as an officer in the Royal Air Force Air Cadets, an organisation whose ethos represents the true spirit of this country. I am proud to be Welsh. I am proud to be British. Two things, as Darren said, that should never be in conflict. I want my children—my two boys—to learn about Henry Tudor, Rorke's Drift and the Falklands war. I want them to know that Wales helped to shape the world that we live in today, the bonds and the sacrifices we have shared, and I want Wales to remain where she belongs, at the very heart and soul of the United Kingdom.

Of course, if Wales was an independent country, it would be the one hundred and thirty seventh largest country in world, sandwiched in size between Mongolia and Uruguay. We also know that countries around the world have a GVA—a measure of the value of goods and services produced in the economy—that is lower than that of Wales: Haiti. So why, having identified that Wales is neither too small nor too poor to be independent, do I oppose independence? The primary reason is straightforward, and it rests on both Wales's tax receipts and its GVA. An independent Wales would, based upon published data, be poorer than we are now, with a combination of higher taxes and poorer public services. 

Plaid Cymru's policy is one of salami-slicing to independence, summed up by 'Devolve, devolve and devolve until there's nothing left to devolve.' Adam Price, when leader of Plaid Cymru, said,

'Plaid Cymru has a simple answer to the challenge posed by Westminster, and that is independence.'

Please ignore that Wales is financially a net beneficiary of the union. We know that because David Phillips of the Institute for Fiscal Studies has estimated that Wales is a net beneficiary of the union by between £12 billion and £15 billion a year. If Wales keeps its revenue and funds its own public spending and then makes a population-based contribution for UK-wide situations, at least understand there would be a large fiscal deficit for Wales. Also according to David Phillips of the IFS, the most recent estimates from the ONS suggest that, for public expenditure, Wales is about 10 per cent higher than across the UK as a whole. This is despite raising substantially less money. We know that, in devolved areas, Wales gets 20 per cent more than England. We know the commission chaired by Gerry Holtham said Wales needs 15 per cent more than England. That is the Barnett floor. Funding cannot fall below that level. The finance Cabinet Minister confirmed that the Holtham committee figure was correct. So, when Wales looks at fair funding, Plaid Cymru, it means we want £1 billion less.

We also know small countries don't have the economic strength to weather financial storms. For example, in Iceland, between 2008 and 2010, a catastrophic financial crash occurred. This involved the default of all three of the country's major privately owned commercial banks in late 2008, following problems in refinancing their short-term debt and a run on deposits. Relative to the size of its economy, Iceland's systematic banking collapse was the largest of any country in economic history. The crisis led to a severe recession and the mass migration of younger people. That's what happens when you play games. It's not those of us who are of retirement age or near retirement age or settled, it's the young people who are forced to leave because there's no employment for them.

I believe in devolution, but not in Welsh independence. We've had seven devolution settlements for Wales, and we're no closer to a long-term settlement than we were before the first. In the UK, we've seen different devolution settlements for Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, as well as different responsibilities devolved to London and some of the larger city regions of England. There are obvious areas that need to be held centrally within a devolved structure, such as defence, foreign affairs, national security, currency, interest rates, overseas aid, immigration, driver and car licensing, central bank and national insurance numbers. If they are not held centrally, that's called independence. Is there any of those that Plaid Cymru do not want devolved on their journey to independence? If those areas are devolved, well that is independence.

Now, should taxation change and there be UK taxes to pay for centrally funded items with all other taxes devolved and collected locally? That's what happens in America for state and national taxes. How will financial support from the wealthier to the poorer regions be organised and maintained? We do not know the direction of devolution.

Not everything needs to be devolved to Wales, Scotland, Northern Ireland or the English city region at the same time. What we should have is a list of items that are available to be devolved, with each Parliament and mayoral area needing at least two thirds of its Members voting in favour for that area to be devolved. This is what happened with policing in Northern Ireland. It was devolved because two thirds of the Northern Ireland Assembly voted for it. This approach avoids big-bang devolution, where control of everything is passed on one day, while still allowing the matter to be devolved as the Parliaments are ready for them and funding is agreed. The advantage of this is that it sets an end point to the devolution journey, outside of creating new countries, and allows each to move at a pace it is comfortable with, with a common end point.

Asymmetric devolution hasn't worked in Britain. It didn't work in Spain. Other countries, like Germany and USA, have the same powers devolved. Each US state has the same powers and responsibility, no matter its size. It's the same with each German Land. But devolution in Wales does not have to end in Cardiff. Devolution in Wales is possible to be devolved to the four regions of Wales and to councils. Which powers would be better devolved to local authorities also needs to be discussed and decided.

The twentieth century is almost a one-way journey of items being taken off local authorities and then dealt with centrally. And I think, really, we want to do what is best for Wales, not what is best for our political views.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Llywydd. Just before I speak, I just wanted to echo what somebody else has said, and I really do think the First Minister should be in the Chamber for what I think is one of the most important debates that we'll have, together with some other Cabinet Members who are missing too.

So, when we debate Wales's place in the United Kingdom, we should do so with our eyes wide open about what separation would actually involve, because this isn't just about flags, slogans or constitutional theory. It is also about people's jobs, pensions, taxes and public services.

So, let's start with the numbers. Some of these have been mentioned already, but I want to go through them again with a little bit more detail. UK public sector debt now stands at almost £3 trillion, okay? There is no agreed formula determining how much of that debt Wales would inherit if it became independent, because that would still have to be negotiated. But just to understand the scale involved, if debt were divided according to population, Wales's share would be around £136 billion. That's approximately £43,000 for every man, woman and child here in Wales, and that's before we even consider Wales's annual finances.

The latest official figures show public expenditure attributed to Wales at around £20,000 per person, whilst revenue raised is only around £13,000. That gap of more than £7,000 per person equates to another figure that was mooted earlier, which is almost £23 billion every single year. Those figures don't tell us exactly what the finances of an independent Wales would look like, and nobody can honestly claim they do, but they do demonstrate the scale of the questions that would have to be answered. Who pays for the NHS? Who pays pensions? What taxes would have to rise? What spending would have to fall? And also, what currency would be used? Nobody seems to know. Who services that debt? And what happens to the fiscal transfers that currently operate across the United Kingdom? Those aren't scare stories; they're legitimate questions involving billions of pounds of taxpayers' money.

But our United Kingdom is about far more than just a balance sheet. Look at the history, some of which has been mentioned earlier, represented by families throughout Wales. Our fathers, grandfathers and great-grandfathers served alongside men and women from England, Scotland and Northern Ireland through two world wars. Welsh regiments fought with extraordinary courage, Welsh communities endured loss and sacrifice, and families waved loved ones goodbye, never knowing whether they would return. They served as part of the armed forces of the United Kingdom, and that shared history matters.

It doesn't dictate what constitutional decisions future generations must make—those decisions belong to us—but neither should we casually dismiss the bonds forged through generations of shared sacrifice, shared endeavour and shared achievements. Those bonds continue today. People cross the Wales and England border every day to work, trade, study, receive healthcare and visit their families. Businesses operate across it, supply chains cross it, families cross it. We share armed forces, we share economic institutions, we share risks. When one part of the United Kingdom needs support, resources can move between its nations and regions.

Wales can proudly and distinctively remain Welsh, whilst remaining part of something bigger too. Our language, our culture, our communities and our national identity do not depend upon erecting a new international border. When independence is proposed, the debate must go beyond the emotional appeal of greater sovereignty. Those advocating fundamental constitutional change need credible answers about debt, the fiscal deficit, pensions, currency, trade, defence and the funding of public services. The numbers involved are simply too large and the consequences too important for anything less. I believe every single one of us in this Chamber has a responsibility to understand the history and the legacy of the United Kingdom that generations before us helped us to build, defend and pass on.

We should think very carefully before taking divisive and potentially irreversible steps without confronting all of the consequences for those who come after us. For my part, I am proud to be Welsh, I am proud to be British, and I will continue to make the case for protecting our place within the United Kingdom, not only because of the history we share, but because of the future we still have the opportunity to build together. Diolch.

contributions.text_english: Thank you very much. We will therefore move immediately to the Cabinet Minister. I call on the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution, Dafydd Trystan Davies.
contributions.text_original: Diolch yn fawr iawn. Symudwn yn syth i'r Gweinidog Cabinet nawr. Galwaf ar y Gweinidog Cabinet dros Effeithiolrwydd Llywodraeth a'r Cyfansoddiad, Dafydd Trystan Davies.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you very much, Llywydd. May I remind everyone in this Chamber that this is a debate that has been called by Reform UK? The First Minister yesterday was talking about health, about childcare, about the economy. Reform UK has chosen to focus on constitutional issues.

But the Government's amendment is a simple one—and I'm pleased to hear that there is support for it from more than one party on the floor of this Chamber—which is that the people of Wales should determine the constitutional future of our country. As we have heard today, Members of this Senedd have different views about where Wales should be constitutionally, and those differences are completely valid in a democratic legislature. But I do hope that we can all agree on two things: that Wales's future should be determined democratically by the people of Wales, and secondly, that Wales should have the powers, the resources and the tools that it needs to deliver on behalf of people here and now. It is these principles that are the basis of the Government's amendment today. Our amendment doesn't ask Members to give up their views; it asks us to acknowledge a principle that hopefully will gain support from across the Chamber, and it is not a party political viewpoint.
contributions.text_original:
Diolch yn fawr iawn, Lywydd. A gaf i atgoffa pawb yn y Siambr hon bod hon yn ddadl sydd wedi'i alw gan Reform UK? Roedd Prif Weinidog Cymru ddoe yn siarad am iechyd, am ofal plant, am yr economi. Reform UK sy'n dewis canolbwyntio ar faterion cyfansoddiadol.

Ond mae gwelliant y Llywodraeth yn un syml—a dwi'n falch i glywed bod yna gefnogaeth iddo fe mewn mwy nag un plaid ar lawr y Siambr yma—sef y dylai pobl Cymru benderfynu ar ddyfodol cyfansoddiadol ein gwlad. Fel rŷn ni wedi'i glywed heddiw, mae gan Aelodau o'r Senedd hon farn wahanol am ble y dylai Cymru fod yn y pen draw yn gyfansoddiadol. Mae'r gwahaniaethau hynny yn gwbl ddilys mewn deddfwrfa ddemocrataidd. Ond dwi'n gobeithio y gallwn ni i gyd gytuno ar ddau beth: y dylai dyfodol Cymru gael ei benderfynu'n ddemocrataidd gan bobl Cymru, ac yn ail, y dylai Cymru gael y pwerau, yr adnoddau a'r offer sydd eu hangen i gyflawni dros bobl yma ac yn awr. Yr egwyddorion hyn sy'n sail i welliant y Llywodraeth heddiw. Dyw ein gwelliant ni ddim yn gofyn i Aelodau roi'r gorau i'w barn; mae'n gofyn i ni gydnabod egwyddor y gobeithiaf y gall ennyn cefnogaeth ar draws y Siambr, a dyw e ddim yn safbwynt pleidiol.

contributions.text_english:
The principle is one that has been widely recognised.

'National aspirations must be respected; peoples may...be...governed only by their own consent.'

That was Woodrow Wilson to Congress in 1918. The self-determination of peoples is in the first article of the UN charter. Talking of our Scottish friends,

'as a nation, they have an undoubted right to national self-determination'.

I didn't expect myself to be quoting Baroness Thatcher approvingly in this Chamber, but she was right, of course—on that matter. [Interruption.] Wait for it. But we must put the people at the heart of constitutional change, because the UK is a 'voluntary nation of nations'—Gordon Brown, the former Prime Minister, in the commission on the UK's future. And yesterday, the Scottish Parliament agreed that

'the Parliament agrees that Scotland...has a right to decide its own future.'

contributions.text_english: If there is one lesson to learn from the last quarter of a century of devolution, it is this: the constitutional settlement is not static. Someone somewhere said that devolution is a process, not an event. The question is not will constitutional change happen; the question is how can we ensure that Wales is ready for that change, can influence it and benefit from it. For this Government, that means practical changes that help us to ensure better results and outcomes for people on the ground and for communities. This is not a theoretical matter, that's not what constitutional change is; it is ensuring that we have the powers, the resources and the tools to deliver for the people of Wales.

Mi ddywedodd rhywun rhywle fod datganoli yn broses, ddim yn ddigwyddiad. Nid y cwestiwn yw a fydd newid cyfansoddiadol yn digwydd; y cwestiwn yw sut y gallwn sicrhau bod Cymru yn barod ar gyfer y newid hwnnw, yn gallu dylanwadu arno ac yn elwa ohono. I'r Llywodraeth hon, mae hynny'n golygu diwygiadau ymarferol sy'n ein helpu ni i sicrhau canlyniadau gwell i bobl ar lawr gwlad ac i gymunedau. Nid mater damcaniaethol yn unig yw diwygio cyfansoddiadol; mae'n sicrhau bod gennym y pwerau, yr adnoddau a'r offer i gyflawni dros bobl Cymru.

contributions.text_english:
That's why our priorities in terms of devolution are clear. We made the case for progress on devolving rail infrastructure, on justice and policing, and on the Crown Estate. These are areas where there is substantial evidence, significant public interest and support that reaches well beyond a single political party. They will lead to a better train service, to lower energy bills, to safer communities—real changes to people's lives here in Wales. I've been heartened by the positive approach from the UK Government in response to those calls, and I hope we can conclude those discussions constructively.

Our objective isn't to move powers between institutions, but to ensure responsibilities sit at the level where they can be exercised most effectively and deliver the best outcomes for people and communities. And let me be clear to my colleagues here: it does indeed mean decentralisation within Wales as part of that package. We are decentralists in Plaid Cymru and we believe in those principles as a key area for us.

Turning to some of the points made in the debate, I do reflect there is a certain irony, particularly from colleagues opposite, in their support for the free movement of goods, capital, services and people, and of a large union that would bring all of those freedoms together. I would remind people that that was voted upon some years ago, and it remains our position that Wales would be better off in such a large European union.

There have also been points about the proud history of Wales, the proud history of Wales in the industrial revolution. And yet we have also heard from the benches opposite that that great nation that powered the industrial revolution—and we've heard of its great success—has fiscal challenges today. That is the legacy of the British state. We've heard about Slovenia, which saw a growth of 33 per cent in its gross domestic product in 10 years. We've heard about other countries who've seen growth far in excess of the Welsh context—successful independent countries—in this debate here.

But let's return to the fundamental point of our amendment and of this debate, in the view of the Government. Members here will disagree as to where Wales should ultimately be heading, but I do sincerely hope that we can agree on some basic fundamentals: that Wales's future should be determined democratically, and that change should be informed by evidence, not assertion. The public debate is stronger when it includes a wide range of voices and perspectives, and it is our shared responsibility to ensure that Wales has the confidence, the capacity and the tools to shape its own future. The people of Wales, Llywydd, are sovereign. It is for us to determine our future, wherever that may lead us. Diolch yn fawr.

contributions.text_english: I call on James Evans to reply to the debate.
contributions.text_original: Galwaf are James Evans i ymateb i'r ddadl.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Llywydd. Can I thank everybody contributing to such a lively debate this afternoon? There's nothing more I love in this Chamber than talking about the second greatest union in my life—other than my marriage, of course—and that is the great union of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, and the great benefits that it brings to the people right the way across these islands.

We opened with Adrian. As you said, we are Welsh, but we are also British. We can be both, and far too often this debate gets polarised between the two. And as we've seen during the election, Plaid Cymru like to politicise Welshness, which is an absolute disgrace. You also raised the point about the United Kingdom being our biggest trading partner. We know that. We know how important the United Kingdom is to us. But what would Plaid Cymru want us to do? They'd want to make us poorer and more reliant on the state, something that we all fundamentally disagree with.

You also raised an important point about defence. That's something that keeps us safe at night. It keeps us safe in our beds, and that is something we should always be proud of. Because, as Darren Millar raised, those are questions that Plaid Cymru simply cannot answer when they're asked about it. They dodge the question because they know they do not know the answer. You did raise the constitutional arrangements of these islands. Yes, they're not perfect, but what is the alternative? Who would we see as a President of Wales? Maybe the ex-Llywydd and Minister may be a candidate, who knows? But I don't think we need to change the arrangements that we currently have. Because Plaid would hold us at the back of the queue, and I think the Minister summed this up. They want to join the EU, but they want to leave another union. The hypocrisy in their argument is absolutely astounding.

contributions.text_english: We'll now move to item 9, the short debate. Anthony Slaughter.
contributions.text_original: Symudwn at eitem 9, y ddadl fer. Anthony Slaughter.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Lywydd. The following Members will be speaking after my opening remarks: Sarah Rees, Natasha Asghar, Matthew Jones, Cristiana Emsley, Huw Thomas and Joe Martin.

Over the past few weeks, my e-mails, like others, have been flooded with messages from people, distraught and disorientated. People who had surgeries cancelled at the eleventh hour with no explanation or option to reschedule. Patients, friends and family members desperate for answers as to why this had happened, what went wrong and how they could move forward.

On Friday, 28 August, three and a half weeks ago, hundreds of patients had their surgeries and surgical assessments suddenly paused while a clinical review was undertaken into Welsh gender services referrals. Many of these patients found out that their surgery would not be taking place while they were already in hospital. These are people who had spent years preparing, both physically and mentally, for this life-affirming surgery, which is recognised by medical organisations, professionals and NHS providers as being clinically effective at improving health outcomes and quality of life. They had jumped through every hoop asked of them, had arranged and rearranged their lives around this day. I listened to people who explained that they were left feeling abandoned, alone and confused, having had the rug pulled from under them at the very last second by the system that is supposed to care for them.

Now, I wasn't planning on sharing this. However, when listening to the stories from my constituents and others, in my own way, I was able to relate to that agonising wait in the days leading up to planned surgery. Over recess, I underwent scheduled and serious surgery. Many of you might have noticed that I was somewhat absent over the summer, and the reason for that was I was preparing for surgery, in hospital and then in recovery. Over the summer, I experienced the reality of what prepping for surgery entailed, the physical and mental stress—something so many here will be able to relate to. When I walked onto that silent ward at 5.00 a.m., the wave of emotion I felt is difficult to put into words—the silence of the sleeping ward, the uncertainty, the fear.

contributions.text_english:
But what does provide solace in those scary moments? It's the knowledge that you are in the place where everyone is working around the clock to treat you, to care for you, to listen to you. You trust the system around you. Now, for some, that trust has been broken. To think that, today, right here in Wales, we have a system that, for a certain group of people, is felt to be actively working in opposition to their well-being is a terrifying thought, one that, had it been something that I had had to consider alongside everything else, would've made my personal experience exponentially so much more traumatic. To think that the right to access health and care for some people in this country is now up for debate is unthinkable. It is not how this system was designed to run.

Now, my personal story is not what's important here. What is important is that the voices and experiences of the trans community are amplified and understood. One of the key principles on which our NHS is based is equal access to healthcare for all, regardless of age, gender or background. Another is that it has a patient-centred approach, putting individuals at the heart of their operations, providing a service that is reflective of their needs and their preferences.

Gender-affirming surgery has been available on the NHS since the 1960s, with thousands of surgeries performed each year. This is not experimental treatment and this should not be considered a controversial area of medicine. It is a well-established and highly studied area of medicine that the NHS has a legal and statutory duty to provide. The decision to pause these surgeries was ill-thought-out and callous. But it also demonstrates a failure of governance within NHS Wales Joint Commissioning Committee and sadly, a breakdown in communication with the Welsh Government. For patients to be told, just hours away from surgery, vulnerable but prepared, that their operation would not be going ahead, with no explanation, no indication of a rescheduled date and with no communication in the days following demonstrates a failure of the duty of care that patients are entitled to during one of the most significant events of their lives—a decision made seemingly without evidence of imminent or direct risk to patients and with no clear safety justification. How have we found ourselves in a situation where some of the supposed core values of the NHS appear to be less applicable to some patients than others? Why is the Welsh Gender Service being punished for being more efficient and effective than its English and Scottish counterparts?

The Welsh Greens are shouting loudly about this, because there's a dangerous precedent that this decision sets for human rights. This is not an ideological debate; everyone in Wales is entitled to NHS healthcare. Gender-affirming healthcare saves lives. We know, based on conversations with key stakeholders in the community, that, in June, the Welsh Gender Service was not aware of any concerns. But just two months later, the drastic escalation was made by the NWJCC to suspend all referrals and surgeries. NHS Wales's very own oversight and escalation framework, section 28, is designed to identify and address emerging issues before they have a material impact. This raises legitimate questions about how this situation rapidly evolved without any oversight or involvement from the Welsh Government. The Welsh Government should never have been surprised by this issue, nor should the NWJCC have been baffled by the discrepancy in referral numbers.

Patients who had their surgeries paused had been referred in 2020, meaning that they'd waited six years just to get to this point, with months of mental and physical preparation for surgery. Now, trans people in this country disproportionately experience poorer mental health, and the impact of this uncertainty and of cancellations have only caused further harm and distrust. Key stakeholder groups and community members have been calling on Welsh Government Ministers to use their powers under the NHS (Wales) Act 2006 to overturn this pause and resume surgery. This was clearly a disproportionate and drastic decision given the lack of evidence of harm or malpractice. So, my question is: what powers do the Welsh Government have to intervene?

The trans community are constantly left fearing that they are an afterthought, that their health and well-being are always under attack, that their right to safety and security in Wales is not a given. What this community needs now more than ever is decisive action—proof that their Government will stand up for them and take the lead, not tiptoe around the edges. The trans community should not be left waiting yet again whilst having to justify their right to healthcare and justify their very existence. Again, this is not up for debate.

When I walked into the Heath this summer with a clear timeline for surgery and recovery, there was not a doubt in my mind that I would be operated on, no doubt that I would be receiving aftercare and that my treatment plan would be thoroughly communicated. To think that there are some patients in Wales for whom that is now not their reality is horrifying. This decision has lost the trust of a vulnerable and consistently targeted group of people. Is this really the future we see in Wales, where healthcare becomes selective? The Welsh Government needs to act now, and I call on the Minister to answer the unanswered questions from community stakeholders. What is the exact nature of the so-called concerns cited by the NWJCC? How do these reflect a clear and immediate risk to patients to the extent that it required overnight cancellation of all planned surgeries?

Second, will the Welsh Government review the failure of governance that led to both patients and the Government being blindsided and put in place robust measures in consultation with the affected stakeholders to hold the NWJCC to account? Will the Welsh Government apologise to the trans community for the clear failure of communication that has left them in this unbearable limbo? Healthcare in Wales must be based on evidence, fairness and dignity, not on uncertainty, fear or political pressure. Diolch.

What is the exact nature of the so-called concerns cited by the NWJCC? How do these reflect a clear and immediate risk to patients to the extent that it required overnight cancellation of all planned surgeries?

Second, will the Welsh Government review the failure of governance that led to both patients and the Government being blindsided and put in place robust measures in consultation with the affected stakeholders to hold the NWJCC to account? Will the Welsh Government apologise to the trans community for the clear failure of communication that has left them in this unbearable limbo? Healthcare in Wales must be based on evidence, fairness and dignity, not on uncertainty, fear or political pressure. Diolch.

Diolch. I speak here as a representative of a recognised, protected minority group, not only for transgender and non-binary people in my own constituency, but for transgender people right across Wales. I heard their voices, almost 100 of whom came to a public meeting that I hosted with Matthew Jones MS in the days after the shocking news of this pause in surgery for Welsh patients, to understand the true impact of this unprecedented action. The strongest thing I heard, 'Nothing about us without us.'

The parameters of the assessment were to ensure that no clinical harm came to patients, yet patients subjected to this review have already faced what the NWJCC have accepted is a significant level of psychiatric harm. The NWJCC have also confirmed today that the pause will remain in place until the necessary clinical assurances have been received. So, I must ask the Minister their question and not mine: are you assured that the evidence gathered by the NWJCC warrants this completely unprecedented pause? And will the Welsh Government individually review how a decision of this magnitude can be made without warning to Government, the Welsh Gender Service, or to patients?

Finally, I call on every decent human being to stand with the trans community. When you hear someone question a person's identity, call it out. This isn't harmless banter. It results in people surviving instead of thriving. Minority groups are not a political tool. Trans lives matter and trans healthcare is a human right.

Before I begin, I'd like to thank the Member for giving me a minute and also I hope that your surgery went well and continues to go well, as well.

The title of this short debate suggests that pausing sex-change operations is unacceptable, but that couldn't be further from the truth. There is nothing unacceptable about pausing irreversible surgery at the Welsh Gender Service while serious concerns are investigated. Clearly, the NHS believes there is a case to answer for here over the abnormally high rates of people being referred for irreversible gender surgeries, hence why this action was taken. Patient safety and well-being should always be the No. 1 priority, and pausing treatment in light of this review is absolutely the right thing to do. This decision was based on clinical and safety concerns, and patients deserve the strongest possible safeguards before a referral is made, yet the rhetoric that I've been hearing and seeing from certain politicians in relation to the current situation of the Welsh Gender Service is deeply worrying and, in my view, amounts to putting ideology before patient safety. The Welsh Gender Service has been referring patients for surgery at rates three to four times higher than clinics across the border in England. That is alarming and must be investigated. So, I would like to ask the Cabinet Minister today: will you confirm the timetable for this review, provide a guarantee that this probe will be genuinely independent and put patient welfare before gender ideology? Thank you.

contributions.text_english: I thank Anthony for this debate. I want to begin by thanking you, Mabon, the Minister. I value every conversation that we've had and I recognise your commitment to standing up for trans people and trying to make sure that this situation is resolved. Also, to all Government Ministers, it's clear that you support trans people. But this decision was made by the NWJCC at arm's length from the Government, and the NWJCC has urgent questions to answer. Its lack of transparency is highly concerning. More than three weeks ago, I wrote, with backbenchers, to the NWJCC with urgent questions about the decision and how people would be supported. We've had no reply. A recent virtual briefing on the pause raised more questions than answers. These have not been answered yet. And today, the NWJCC sent some Members a list of FAQs about its review process, but not to me—I've had to have it from another Member. The FAQs raise even further questions about the timeline, which I want the NWJCC to answer. If they've reviewed all the patients and are satisfied, or aren't satisfied, what next? At what point will the pause stop? Is it 10 patients, or 60? Is it for patients registered for surgery in 2027? Many people have put their lives on hold, including taking months off work to recover after surgery. Their health, livelihoods and finances are all now in limbo. We must reassure a community already experiencing fear and anxiety, made worse because the NWJCC has not publicly or adequately explained their concerns. Any independent review must quickly provide answers to those awaiting surgery and restore confidence across the wider trans community. Diolch.

contributions.text_english: Thank you, Llywydd. In line with your instructions, I'll keep this very brief, and I'd like to thank the Member for allowing me this intervention. Whatever our political differences, truth and patient safety must unite us. I accept that this pause may cause distress and patients must be supported, but what would be unacceptable is continuing irreversible referrals when serious concerns exist about referral appropriateness, clinical governance and patient safeguards—concerns I have already raised directly with the Cabinet Minister for health. As lawmakers, our duty is therefore not to pressure clinicians towards a preferred conclusion, it is to safeguard their clinical independence, to follow the science and the evidence, wherever they lead. Distress demands compassion and support, but compassion cannot lower the evidential threshold for irreversible treatment. Medicine demands evidence. Patient safety demands both. Thank you.

Thank you very much. May I distance myself and the Government from the comments made by Joe Martin, which are entirely unacceptable in the context of today's debate? May I also thank the Member for bringing forward this important debate and wish him well on his journey towards a full recovery?

This is the first real opportunity for the Senedd to discuss this matter and for me to place our response on the record. Firstly, I would like to acknowledge the pain and distress that many have felt since the decision was announced. For many, this was seen as another decision in a long series of decisions to strip trans people of their rights, eroding their very identity, and I understand these concerns and fears. So, let me emphasise that this was a clinical decision, made on the basis of clinical evidence without political intervention. Let me also be clear that we—that I—stand with the trans community.

As a Government, we are committed to safeguarding the rights of every LGBTQ+ person in Wales, and, as Members know, Plaid Cymru played a key role in ensuring the delivery of the LGBTQ+ action plan. Our manifesto sets out our commitment to the trans community, and you can be assured that the Welsh Government stands with the trans community and will continue to defend the rights of trans people in line with our commitment to a welcoming and inclusive Wales.

I recognise that some people accessing gender identity services will already be experiencing emotional distress, and I understand the additional distress, anxiety and uncertainty of this situation. I want to be clear that we remain committed to ensuring access to high-quality specialist gender identity services in Wales. I also want to reassure people that this decision is a temporary pause, not a stop, and a decision made by the NHS Wales Joint Commissioning Committee in the interest of patient safety.

The decision to pause gender-affirming surgery was made through established clinical governance processes. These apply to all services commissioned by the NHS Wales Joint Commissioning Committee. It isn't unusual for the JCC to place services in escalation when there is a need to seek assurance on clinical or quality issues. These processes exist to ensure patient safety, and we need to be led by them, based on their independent clinical assessment of the evidence.

Welsh Ministers don't have a role in the clinical governance and escalation processes within the JCC. The NHS Wales Joint Commissioning Committee are responsible for the commissioning and oversight of specialised services, including gender identity services, and are formally accountable to health boards in Wales. This provides a consistency of offer, with the necessary governance and monitoring and clinical oversight in place to ensure services are safe and effective. The JCC brings together health boards for services that need to be commissioned once for Wales. This includes specialist gender identity services. As a Government, we have been clear that we will be led by the evidence when it comes to ensuring the quality and safety of our NHS services. This is vital if we are to ensure safe services and good outcomes for our patients in Wales.

For the avoidance of doubt, and let me be clear, this was a clinically-led decision made by the JCC due to concerns with the quality of assessments and the volume of referrals for gender surgery. The decision was primarily based on data provided by the gender dysphoria national referral support services. Gender surgery for Welsh patients is commissioned by NHS England, who are responsible for managing and validating referrals for surgery. The centrally held data showed higher rates of referral from Wales, but lower rates of progression to some surgeries. Concerns were also raised by clinical colleagues in NHS England about appropriateness of referrals and clinical suitability. The JCC has a duty of care to all patients who receive specialist services that it commissions to ensure that those services are safe and effective. Taken together, these concerns highlighted potential issues that the JCC needed to take seriously.

Given the level of concerns across parties, I'm grateful that the JCC offered technical briefing sessions to all parties to provide more information about the data and the decisions taken. I hope you took the opportunity to engage in these sessions with the JCC to seek assurances on the questions or concerns that you have.

Following the escalation of the service, the JCC committed to an urgent clinical review of those individuals on the waiting list for gender-affirming surgery. The JCC has already appointed the independent clinical review panel, and, subject to final governance approval, it is anticipated that the review will commence imminently. This review will prioritise those individuals who are further along the pathway to allow appropriate referrals to proceed as soon as possible. The JCC has identified that approximately 60 patients were due surgery between the pausing of surgery in August and the end of December. Our priority is to bring certainty to these people as quickly as possible, and the JCC are confident that all 60 of these cases can be reviewed before the end of December.

There is also a wider, independent review of the Welsh Gender Service. It was always intended by the JCC that this planned review would follow the independent Levy review, which looked at adult gender identity services in England. The independent review has already commenced and comprises both quality and clinical governance elements. The review will focus primarily on assessment, referral and non-surgical aspects of the pathway, while considering relevant pathway interfaces. It will engage key stakeholders, including health boards, partner organisations, patients and carers. Initial findings are expected later this year, with recommendations to be reported to the JCC thereafter.

Both reviews will include independent reviewers and are a clinical process. It is entirely consistent with existing governance arrangements of this nature that the Welsh Government will have no role or involvement in these reviews or the recommendations that they make. We will, of course, expect that both the JCC and Cardiff and Vale University Health Board act on the findings from the reviews as a matter of priority.

I've met with the JCC and been clear that the urgent clinical review needs to be swift to minimise the disruption and distress for individuals on the waiting list. I've also been clear that I expect all patients impacted by this pause to have access to the necessary support whilst the review is undertaken. This includes emotional and psychological support. I've written to Cardiff and Vale University Health Board and received assurances about the support available for those who are affected by the pause.

The JCC has now published the equality and Welsh language impact assessment and the quality impact assessment and other papers related to the decisions on their website.

contributions.text_english:
I acknowledge the distress and uncertainty that this pause has caused for those affected. I have heard personally from people affected by this decision, and I'm grateful to colleagues in the Senedd for their actions in listening to, supporting and advocating on behalf of so many people. I'm working with the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice and Equality to ensure that the impact on the trans community is fully considered as the JCC and Cardiff and Vale University Health Board undertake the review and follow-up work.

I'm being regularly updated on progress by the JCC and Cardiff and Vale University Health Board, and officials met with the JCC yesterday to receive a progress update. I expect any necessary steps to be taken forward as a priority to ensure that the Welsh Gender Service delivers the quality of service that we would all expect.

I'm committed to ensuring that our public bodies provide the highest level of service to everyone who relies on them. With that in mind, it is essential that we continue to learn from decisions such as this one, therefore, I have asked the chief medical officer to conduct a reflective exercise regarding the processes associated with this decision. This will consider methods of communication with patients and others, the timing of that communication and the supporting processes, including the voice of the trans community. The voices of the trans community will be central to this review. Listening and learning are essential.

So, thank you once again, Anthony, for presenting this debate, and thank you to everyone who has contributed in a constructive manner to this debate.

Rwy'n cydnabod y trallod a'r ansicrwydd y mae'r seibiant hwn yn ei achosi i'r rhai yr effeithir arnynt.
